analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand how health systems in Sub-Saharan Africa respond to re-emerging infectious diseases, highlighting the need to address the region's vulnerability to outbreaks such as measles.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed health system resilience in 25 Sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to 2023, using a multidimensional resilience index and a first-order Markov state-transition framework to assess system performance over time.
analysis.methods: The research employed a multinomial logistic regression model to evaluate factors influencing health system resilience, including health expenditure per capita, domestic health-financing share, GDP per capita, and internal armed conflict.
analysis.main_results: Country-year observations were classified into Low, Moderate, or High Resilience categories, with Southern and Eastern Africa showing stronger resilience profiles than Western and Central Africa, where Central Africa had the highest concentration of Low-Resilience countries.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that resilience is dynamic and unevenly distributed, with economic and political factors playing a critical role in determining health system capacity to respond to infectious diseases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform policy decisions on strengthening domestic health financing, improving economic capacity, and enhancing political stability to build more resilient health systems against re-emerging infectious diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's abstract-only evidence limits the depth of analysis, and the resilience classification is based on aggregated indicators, which may not capture nuanced variations in health system performance.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the resilience of health systems in 25 Sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to 2023, focusing on their response to re-emerging infectious diseases like measles. Using a multidimensional resilience index and a first-order Markov state-transition framework, the research classifies country-year observations into Low, Moderate, or High Resilience categories. Results show that Southern and Eastern Africa have stronger resilience profiles compared to Western and Central Africa, with the latter having the highest concentration of Low-Resilience countries. The study highlights that resilience is dynamic and shaped by factors such as health expenditure, economic capacity, and political stability. Policy recommendations emphasize strengthening domestic health financing, targeting Moderate-Resilience countries for improvement, and supporting conflict-affected systems. The findings suggest that health system resilience is unevenly distributed and influenced by sustained financing and stability. However, the abstract-only evidence and reliance on aggregated indicators limit the depth of analysis, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在了解撒哈拉以南非洲国家如何应对再出现的传染病,强调需要解决该地区对暴发(如麻疹)的脆弱性问题。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究分析了2000年至2023年间撒哈拉以南非洲25个国家的卫生系统韧性,采用多维韧性指数和一阶马尔可夫状态转移框架来评估系统随时间的变化表现。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究采用多分类逻辑回归模型来评估影响卫生系统韧性的因素,包括人均卫生支出、国内卫生筹资占比、人均GDP以及内部武装冲突。
elements_zh.main_results: 国家-年份观察结果被分为低韧性、中等韧性和高韧性三类,其中南部和东部非洲表现出更强的韧性特征,而西部和中部非洲的韧性较弱,中部非洲拥有最多的低韧性国家。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,韧性是动态的且分布不均的,经济和政治因素在决定卫生系统应对传染病的能力方面起着关键作用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为政策决策提供了信息,以加强国内卫生筹资、提高经济能力并增强政治稳定性,从而构建更具韧性的卫生系统以应对再出现的传染病。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅基于摘要的证据限制了分析的深度,且韧性分类基于聚合指标,可能无法捕捉卫生系统表现的细微差异。

papers.abstract_zh: 撒哈拉以南非洲(SSA)面临再出现传染病的反复威胁,包括埃博拉病毒病、霍乱、麻疹、拉沙热和马尔堡病毒病。本研究利用多维韧性指数和一阶马尔可夫状态转移框架,评估了2000年至2023年间撒哈拉以南非洲25个国家卫生系统的韧性。国家-年份观察结果根据流行病学表现、卫生筹资、监测、响应能力及恢复指标被分类为低韧性、中等韧性或高韧性。韧性表现出异质性和路径依赖性。低韧性观察结果在随后一年有82.4%的概率保持在低韧性状态,仅有3.1%的概率直接跃迁至高韧性。中等韧性观察结果有19.1%的概率跃迁至高韧性,同时有18.2%的概率下降至低韧性。高韧性观察结果有63.6%的概率保持高韧性,但有36.4%的概率出现倒退。多分类逻辑回归分析表明,人均卫生支出、国内卫生筹资占比和人均GDP与高韧性呈正相关,而内部武装冲突则与高韧性呈负相关。南部和东部非洲表现出更强的韧性特征,而西部和中部非洲的韧性较弱,其中中部非洲拥有最多的低韧性国家。这些发现表明,韧性是动态的、分布不均的,并且受到持续筹资、经济能力和政治稳定等因素的强烈影响。政策优先事项包括加强国内卫生筹资、针对中等韧性国家加速改善、支持受冲突影响的卫生系统,以及协调区域监测和应急响应机制。

papers.title: Editorial: Mathematical Modelling and data analysis in infectious diseases
papers.abstract: Infectious diseases spread through a complex mix of factors: pathogens, hosts, behavior, mobility, environment, health systems, and interventions, all of which interact with each other. Mathematical models and data analysis are essential tools for understanding and scientifically mimicking (simulating) these interactions.These approaches enable researchers to draw robust conclusions from incomplete data, formalize competing hypotheses regarding pathogen transmissions and intervention effects, and integrate diverse sources of evidence to generate forecasts and support evidence-based decision-making. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the use of these tools on an unprecedented scale, with mathematical models informing decisions regarding lockdowns, vaccine allocations, and healthcare capacity-based planning in near real time. But the pandemic also made clear that good models need clear and evidence-based assumptions, must be tested against real data, should be checked against new data whenever possible, and must be used with an understanding of their uncertainty, not treated as perfect predictions [1][2][3]. The challenge has only grown since: infectious-disease data are increasingly high-dimensional and multimodal, spanning genomic surveillance, mobility traces, wastewater signals, and electronic health records, while the methodological toolkit available to analyze them has expanded just as quickly, from classical compartmental models to machine learning and stochastic optimization.The Research Topic Mathematical Modelling and Data Analysis in Infectious Diseases responds to this landscape by bringing together 22 contributions spanning public health, applied mathematics, infectiousdisease epidemiology, and microbial sciences. The collection covers a wide range of approaches: mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied across diseases including COVID-19, influenza, measles, mumps, dengue, and other pathogens of public health concern. Its unifying message is simple: no single method suffices for every question. Instead, the choice of method should follow from the decision at hand, the process generating the data, the observations actually available, and the consequences of incorrect inference or prediction.Several contributions in this collection address a central challenge in infectious-disease surveillance: extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from data that evolve in real time.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study highlights the complexity of infectious disease transmission, emphasizing the interplay of pathogens, hosts, behavior, environment, and interventions. It underscores the need for robust tools to understand these interactions and inform public health decisions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This editorial presents a collection of 22 contributions that span various disciplines, including public health, applied mathematics, and microbial sciences, focusing on the use of mathematical modeling and data analysis in infectious diseases.
analysis.methods: The editorial outlines a range of methodologies, including mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied to diseases such as measles, influenza, dengue, and others.
analysis.main_results: The collection demonstrates the application of diverse analytical approaches to infectious diseases, with specific examples including measles virus and its associated data and modeling techniques.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The editorial interprets the findings as a call for methodological diversity, stating that no single approach is sufficient for all questions and that the choice of method should be guided by the specific context and data available.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of integrating multiple analytical methods to improve surveillance, forecasting, and decision-making in public health, particularly for diseases like measles.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on an editorial review, which does not present original data or results. The assessment is moderate as it reflects a synthesis of existing research rather than new empirical findings.

analysis.summary_en: This editorial discusses the importance of mathematical modeling and data analysis in understanding infectious disease transmission, emphasizing the need for diverse methodologies to address complex public health challenges. It highlights the application of these tools to diseases such as measles, influenza, and dengue, and underscores the limitations of relying on a single method for all questions. The editorial calls for a tailored approach to method selection based on the specific context and data available, which has implications for improving surveillance and decision-making in infectious disease management.

elements_zh.main_results: 该系列展示了多种分析方法在传染病中的应用,具体例子包括麻疹病毒及其相关数据和建模技术。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本编者按将这些发现解读为对方法多样性的呼吁,指出没有单一方法能解决所有问题,方法的选择应根据具体情境和可用数据进行指导。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现强调了整合多种分析方法的重要性,以提高监测、预测和公共卫生决策的质量,特别是在像麻疹这样的疾病中。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 这些证据基于编者按的综述,未提供原始数据或结果。评估为中等强度,因为它反映了现有研究的综合,而非新的实证发现。

analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 这些证据基于编者按的综述,未提供原始数据或结果。评估为中等强度,因为它反映了现有研究的综合,而非新的实证发现。

news.content: Measles Brain Persistence and Lethal SSPE Progression Therapy Area Allergy & Immunology Cardiology Dermatology Diabetes Flagship Journal Gastroenterology General Healthcare Hematology Hepatology Innovations Interventional Cardiology Microbiology & Infectious Diseases Nephrology Neurology Oncology Radiology Reproductive Health Respiratory Rheumatology Urology Podcasts Journals Webinars Congress Hub Toolkit Paediatric Growth Calculator DVT Risk Calculator Due Date Calculator Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) Calculator BMI Calculator Collaborate About EQOH Careers Contact Us Media Pack Editorial Enquiries Contributors & Authors Submit a Paper Media Partners Work With Us EMJ Interactive EMJ GOLD CME search Join FREE This site is intended for healthcare professionals You must accept all conditions before being able to view the post Continue EUR USA EUR USA Therapy Area Allergy & Immunology Cardiology Dermatology Diabetes Flagship Journal Gastroenterology General Healthcare Hematology Hepatology Innovations Interventional Cardiology Microbiology & Infectious Diseases Nephrology Neurology Oncology Radiology Reproductive Health Respiratory Rheumatology Urology Podcasts Journals Webinars Congress Hub Toolkit Paediatric Growth Calculator DVT Risk Calculator Due Date Calculator Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) Calculator BMI Calculator Collaborate About EQOH Careers Contact Us Media Pack Editorial Enquiries Contributors & Authors Submit a Paper Media Partners Work With Us EMJ Interactive EMJ GOLD CME Join FREE Search type Keyword Author Home Neurology Measles in the Brain: How Mutated Viruses Trigger Fatal SSPE Measles in the Brain: How Mutated Viruses Trigger Fatal SSPE 23 Sep 2026 Neurology General Healthcare View All News Key Summary: Measles virus adapts to neural tissue lacking standard receptors via genomic mutations. Mutations in matrix and fusion proteins enable measles to spread across neuronal synapses. SSPE incidence reaches 1 in 600 infant measles cases, leaving vaccination as sole defense. MEASLES outbreaks raise clinical concern over fatal neurological persistence driven by adaptive viral mutations in the human brain. As pediatric vaccination coverage declines and community transmission escalates across the United States, clinicians face an impending wave of delayed, devastating neuropathology. The primary threat centers on subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a slow, progressive, and invariably lethal neurodegenerative disorder. While acute measles virus typically targets immune and respiratory epithelial cells through SLAMF1 and nectin-4 receptors, the central nervous system lacks these canonical entry proteins. Instead, measles virus enters neural parenchyma through trans-endocytosis from airway epithelia to olfactory neurons or via hematogenous spread across the blood-brain barrier. Adaptive Mutations Drive Measles Neurovirulence Once localized within brain tissue, measles virus overcomes the absence of classical receptors through remarkable collective genome evolution. Deep sequencing reveals that viral survival relies on collective infectious units, where complementary genome populations coreplicate within individual cells. Rather than existing as single virions, these assemblies accumulate coordinated alterations within the viral membrane fusion apparatus. Approximately seventy percent of clinical cases exhibit complete matrix protein inactivation, disrupting normal virion assembly while promoting deeper parenchymal penetration. Concurrently, universal alterations in the fusion protein cytoplasmic tail and ectodomain destabilization permit viral activation in cis by synaptic adhesion molecules, including CADM1 and CADM2. These hyperfusogenic properties facilitate direct, cell-to-cell viral transmission across synapses without generating cell-free virus. Clinical Progression and Preventive Imperatives The neurological trajectory of measles virus persistence follows four distinct clinical stages. Early manifestations present insidiously with cognitive decline and behavioral shifts, frequently progressing unnoticed for months. Stage II ushers in hallmark myoclonic jerks, seizures, and characteristic periodic complexes on electroencephalography, accompanied by diagnostic intrathecal measles antibody production. As widespread cortical degradation ensues in stages III and IV, patients deteriorate into spasticity, coma, and vegetative states. Surviving two years post-diagnosis remains below fifty percent. analysis.event: The article reports on measles virus mutations that allow it to persist in the central nervous system, leading to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a fatal neurodegenerative disorder. This is a confirmed scientific finding based on research and clinical observations.

analysis.brief_en: The article published on 2026-09-23 by EMJ explores how measles virus mutations enable it to persist in the central nervous system, leading to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a fatal neurodegenerative disorder. It highlights that SSPE occurs in approximately 1 in 600 infant measles cases and is a growing concern in the United States due to declining vaccination rates. The virus adapts to neural tissue by overcoming the absence of standard receptors through genomic changes, allowing it to spread across synapses without generating cell-free virus. Clinical progression involves four stages, with severe outcomes including spasticity, coma, and vegetative states. Survival rates remain below fifty percent two years post-diagnosis, and current treatments are largely ineffective. The article underscores the importance of universal measles vaccination as the only validated defense against this neurological complication. The findings are based on scientific research and clinical data, with no indication of unresolved information.

analysis_en.event: The article reports on measles virus mutations that allow it to persist in the central nervous system, leading to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a fatal neurodegenerative disorder. This is a confirmed scientific finding based on research and clinical observations.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: SSPE incidence reaches 1 in 600 infant measles cases. The risk is described as high, with survival rates below fifty percent two years post-diagnosis. The article also highlights the potential for an impending wave of delayed neuropathology due to declining vaccination coverage.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The article discusses the lack of effective antiviral agents and immunomodulators against established collective units of the virus. It emphasizes universal measles vaccination as the only validated defense. The evidence is based on scientific research and clinical data, with no indication of unresolved information.

news.title_zh: 麻疹在大脑中的作用:突变病毒如何引发致命的亚急性硬化性全脑炎(SSPE)- EMJ
news.source_body_en: The article published on 2026-09-23 by EMJ explores how measles virus mutations enable it to persist in the central nervous system, leading to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a fatal neurodegenerative disorder. It highlights that SSPE occurs in approximately 1 in 600 infant measles cases and is a growing concern in the United States due to declining vaccination rates. The virus adapts to neural tissue by overcoming the absence of standard receptors through genomic changes, allowing it to spread across synapses without generating cell-free virus. Clinical progression involves four stages, with severe outcomes including spasticity, coma, and vegetative states. Survival rates remain below fifty percent two years post-diagnosis, and current treatments are largely ineffective. The article underscores the importance of universal measles vaccination as the only validated defense against this neurological complication. The findings are based on scientific research and clinical data, with no indication of unresolved information.

news.content: News Sports Lifestyle Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Public Notices HEALTHCARE Exclusive: Measles cases spreading through PA, including Somerset area Madolin Edwards The Daily American Sept. 22, 2026, 11:30 a.m. ET Pennsylvania has reported over 760 measles cases in 2026, with four resulting in death. Health officials attribute the rise in cases to lower vaccination rates in some communities. Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air, causing fever, cough, and a distinct rash. The MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles, with two doses recommended for children. Somerset County has not been immune to the rise of measles cases in the state. More than 760 cases of measles have been reported in Pennsylvania so far in 2026 and the number continues to rise. Somerset County stood at 13 cases as of Sept. 21. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, as of Sept. 18, 767 measles cases were confirmed across 38 counties. There had been 36 new positive cases since Sept. 16, and 150 people have been hospitalized. Of those cases, only four are vaccinated individuals, or less than 1% of the cases. Four people have been confirmed by the state to have died because of measles-associated complications. Why is measles on the rise? The effectiveness of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine caused measles to be declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. However, outbreaks have surged in recent years. "We are seeing lower vaccination rates in certain communities," said Mark Yaros, M.D., vice president of medical affairs at UPMC Somerset, in an email. "Most people are protected through community immunity, when more than 95% of people in that community are vaccinated. When the percentage of people fully vaccinated falls below 95%, that is when outbreaks are most likely to occur. "It’s hard to pinpoint exactly why people are leery of getting vaccinations, especially when the MMR vaccine has a strong safety record." What is measles? Measles is a serious, extremely contagious disease caused by the measles virus. Common measles symptoms include a high fever, cough and rash. The rash usually appears three to five days after symptoms begin and begins as flat spots at the hairline before moving downward to the rest of the body. The spots can join as the rash moves downward, and raised bumps may also appear on top of the spots. The fever can spike to over 104 F after the rash appears. It is most common in children but can occur in adults. According to UPMC, the measles virus spreads through the air when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The measles virus can survive in the air or on a surface for up to two hours, making it very contagious. Someone with measles can infect up to 90% of unprotected people around them. People can spread measles before they even know they're sick. An infected person can spread measles from four days before the rash appears until four days afterward. People who are immunocompromised may be contagious even longer. Flu-like symptoms typically begin about seven to 14 days after exposure to the measles virus. It can sometimes take up to three weeks. There are no specific treatments for measles other than managing measles symptoms and complications. Those infected should avoid contact with others and stay home from work, school, and other locations, according to the DOH. Most people with measles can recover at home. Measles symptoms typically last for one to two weeks. If complications develop, it can take several weeks to recover. The infected person should remain isolated for at least four days after the rash appears. They are recommended to talk to their doctor about when to return to normal activities. Should we be vaccinated? The best way to prevent measles infection is with the MMR vaccine. Children between 12 months and 12 years of age can get the vaccine, which also protects against chickenpox. Two doses of the MMR and MMRV vaccine are recommended. Measles can cause serious, life-threatening symptoms and complications in people who aren’t protected against the disease. The people most at risk of measles infection include unvaccinated people and vaccinated people who didn’t develop immunity. People who are most at risk of measles complications include adults over age 20; children under age 5; malnourished people; people with compromised immune systems and pregnant women who can also spread measles to their child during pregnancy. MMR vaccine is available across the state by contacting a health care provider, county or municipal health department, DOH State Health Center, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), or a Vaccines for Children (VFC) program. Should older people who received the MMR vaccination to go to school get a booster or revaccinated? Yaros said this is a conversation that should be occurring between an individual and their physician. "In general those born before 1957 are considered immune and do not need an additional dose of vaccine," he said. "For those born after 1957, if they have documentation of receiving two doses of live measles-containing vaccine or laboratory evidence of disease, they do not need another dose of the vaccine." The recommended vaccine schedule is the first dose given when a child is 12 to 15 months old and the second dose given when a child is 4 to 6 years old. Unvaccinated older children, adolescents, and adults can also get vaccinated with two doses of the MMR vaccine, delivered at least 28 days apart. For those people who have been exposed to measles and are unvaccinated, vaccination is recommended within three days of exposure. Doctors can typically diagnose measles from the rash and other symptoms. They will also take blood and other samples for laboratory testing to confirm the diagnosis. "These vaccines have strong safety records, and the illnesses they prevent can be far more serious than the temporary side effects associated with vaccination," Yaros said. "No vaccine is 100% effective at preventing infection, and no vaccine is totally free of side effects, but ample evidence shows MMR vaccination significantly reduces the risk of severe disease and hospitalization. "Outbreaks like this validate the benefits of being vaccinated. People who are vaccinated may still become infected, but their risk is generally lower than those who are unvaccinated, and their risk of serious illness is substantially reduced." For more information on measles and the MMR vaccine, go to https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles. analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials are attributing the rise in cases to lower vaccination rates. Over 767 cases were confirmed across 38 counties, with 150 hospitalizations and four deaths. Health officials attribute the rise to lower vaccination rates in some communities. The measles virus is highly contagious, spreading through the air and surviving for up to two hours on surfaces. It can infect up to 90% of unprotected individuals. The MMR vaccine is the most effective prevention method, with two doses recommended for children. Unvaccinated individuals and those without immunity are at higher risk, especially adults over 20, children under 5, and immunocompromised people. Health authorities are urging vaccination and advising those exposed to seek medical attention within three days. The situation remains under investigation, with ongoing efforts to manage the spread and protect vulnerable populations.

(Jose F. Moreno/The Philadelphia Inquirer/TNS) By Michael Urban | murban@republicanherald.com | Republican Herald PUBLISHED: September 25, 2026 at 3:20 PM EDT | UPDATED: September 25, 2026 at 4:16 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... With the state this week confirming Schuylkill County’s first measles case in more than two decades, local school districts have been planning for students potentially coming to school with the virus. Until Monday, there had been no verified cases of measles in Schuylkill since at least 2003, when the state began keeping electronic disease records. Schuylkill was the 39th county where measles was confirmed this year in Pennsylvania. The Keystone State has had 835 cases and four measles-attributed deaths, according to state officials. In the wake of that news about a local case, Schuylkill school administrators spoke this week about how their districts keep detailed vaccination and immunization records for students and have established procedures for responding to any communicable disease concerns, including measles. Pennsylvania specifically directs schools to coordinate with the state Department of Health or local health department when addressing suspected measles cases, said Shawn Fitzpatrick, Schuylkill Haven superintendent. “If a potential measles case were identified within our schools, our nursing team would work closely with the Pennsylvania Department of Health and follow its guidance regarding appropriate notification, monitoring, exclusion and other necessary measures,” he said. Williams Valley has also shared the state’s measles guidance with its school nurses and principals, including how to review immunization records, isolate a student who appears ill, notify public health officials and follow department of health direction if a case is confirmed, said acting Superintendent Paul Caputo. “We are not waiting for a case in our buildings to take this seriously,” he said. “Our school nurses are the first line. They know the signs to watch for, which students have documented immunity, and they know to isolate a symptomatic student and have the family call the provider before walking into a waiting room. If a case were confirmed, we would immediately work with the county and the state health department on who was exposed and what comes next.” Caputo advised parents to confirm that their child’s MMR vaccinations — which protect them against measles, mumps and rubella — are up to date and to keep sick children home, since measles is highly contagious. “People can spread it before the rash appears,” he said. “If their child has a fever with a cough, runny nose or red, watery eyes, call the doctor before you go in and tell the office you are concerned about measles.” Pine Grove School District nurses have been following the statewide measles reports closely, and this week’s confirmation of a case in Schuylkill brought the issue a little closer to home, said Pine Grove Superintendent Heath Renninger. District officials and nurses have begun talking about how to respond if a case occurs within its schools, and they are up to date on state recommendations, he said. “Our goal is to stay informed, be prepared and respond appropriately based on the guidance we receive,” he said. Measles had been declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, meaning it had not continuously spread for more than a year. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention credited that achievement to a highly effective use of the MMR vaccine. But measles cases have been rising in the U.S. since early 2025, which health officials attribute to a recent drop in MMR vaccination rates. So far in 2026, there have been 835 measles cases in Pennsylvania, and that number grew by 129 this week, according to the state’s online measles dashboard. A total of 164 of those patients required hospitalization, and the four measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania that have occurred since late August were the first deaths caused by the virus in the state in 35 years, state officials said. The CDC, however, has different criteria for tallying measles deaths and has not included Pennsylvania’s four fatalities in its national count. Each of the counties that border Schuylkill also has measles cases. As cases continue to spread in Pennsylvania, the Department of Health is working closely with school district administrators and nurses to ensure they have the information and guidance they need, said Stephanie Nojiri, deputy press secretary. “Since the majority of students (more than 93%) are fully vaccinated, most schools benefit from robust community immunity that serves as a powerful shield against the virus,” Nojiri said. “To further empower families and maintain transparency, the department recently published a first-of-its-kind online school-level vaccination data tool so parents can make informed health and educational decisions.” Nearly 1,000 school nurses in Pennsylvania also attended in-person and live virtual medical briefings the department hosted this summer to help healthcare providers identify and treat patients with measles, she said. Pennsylvania’s secretaries of health and education have written multiple letters to all Pennsylvania schools about the importance of vaccine requirements for children attending school to help increase immunization reporting and reduce vaccine-preventable diseases, she said. These letters also reminded school leaders of their responsibility under the law to submit vaccine data to the department by Dec. 31 every year. The departments are partnering with non-reporting schools to achieve higher rates of reporting, while collaborating with local healthcare providers to expand access to routine immunization across the state, she said. Measles symptoms usually start seven to 14 days after contact with the virus, according to the Mayo Clinic. The illness begins with a high fever, dry cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by tiny white spots inside the mouth and a distinct red rash that spreads downward from the face. Local hospitals urge anyone who is unvaccinated, or whose children have not been vaccinated, to get the MMR vaccine as soon as possible, since measles can cause serious health complications in the near- and long-term. Babies, children and those with underlying health problems are especially vulnerable. Also at risk are those who cannot be vaccinated because they are undergoing cancer treatments or have other health issues. One in 5 who acquire the virus require hospitalization, and some who get it when they’re young have lifelong complications, health officials said. Moreno/The Philadelphia Inquirer/TNS) By Michael Urban | murban@republicanherald.com | Republican Herald PUBLISHED: September 25, 2026 at 3:20 PM EDT | UPDATED: September 25, 2026 at 4:16 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... With the state this week confirming Schuylkill County’s first measles case in more than two decades, local school districts have been planning for students potentially coming to school with the virus. Until Monday, there had been no verified cases of measles in Schuylkill since at least 2003, when the state began keeping electronic disease records. Schuylkill was the 39th county where measles was confirmed this year in Pennsylvania. The Keystone State has had 835 cases and four measles-attributed deaths, according to state officials. In the wake of that news about a local case, Schuylkill school administrators spoke this week about how their districts keep detailed vaccination and immunization records for students and have established procedures for responding to any communicable disease concerns, including measles. Pennsylvania specifically directs schools to coordinate with the state Department of Health or local health department when addressing suspected measles cases, said Shawn Fitzpatrick, Schuylkill Haven superintendent. “If a potential measles case were identified within our schools, our nursing team would work closely with the Pennsylvania Department of Health and follow its guidance regarding appropriate notification, monitoring, exclusion and other necessary measures,” he said. Williams Valley has also shared the state’s measles guidance with its school nurses and principals, including how to review immunization records, isolate a student who appears ill, notify public health officials and follow department of health direction if a case is confirmed, said acting Superintendent Paul Caputo. “We are not waiting for a case in our buildings to take this seriously,” he said. “Our school nurses are the first line. They know the signs to watch for, which students have documented immunity, and they know to isolate a symptomatic student and have the family call the provider before walking into a waiting room. If a case were confirmed, we would immediately work with the county and the state health department on who was exposed and what comes next.” Caputo advised parents to confirm that their child’s MMR vaccinations — which protect them against measles, mumps and rubella — are up to date and to keep sick children home, since measles is highly contagious. “People can spread it before the rash appears,” he said. “If their child has a fever with a cough, runny nose or red, watery eyes, call the doctor before you go in and tell the office you are concerned about measles.” Pine Grove School District nurses have been following the statewide measles reports closely, and this week’s confirmation of a case in Schuylkill brought the issue a little closer to home, said Pine Grove Superintendent Heath Renninger. District officials and nurses have begun talking about how to respond if a case occurs within its schools, and they are up to date on state recommendations, he said. “Our goal is to stay informed, be prepared and respond appropriately based on the guidance we receive,” he said. Measles had been declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, meaning it had not continuously spread for more than a year. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention credited that achievement to a highly effective use of the MMR vaccine. But measles cases have been rising in the U.S. since early 2025, which health officials attribute to a recent drop in MMR vaccination rates. So far in 2026, there have been 835 measles cases in Pennsylvania, and that number grew by 129 this week, according to the state’s online measles dashboard. A total of 164 of those patients required hospitalization, and the four measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania that have occurred since late August were the first deaths caused by the virus in the state in 35 years, state officials said. The CDC, however, has different criteria for tallying measles deaths and has not included Pennsylvania’s four fatalities in its national count. Each of the counties that border Schuylkill also has measles cases. As cases continue to spread in Pennsylvania, the Department of Health is working closely with school district administrators and nurses to ensure they have the information and guidance they need, said Stephanie Nojiri, deputy press secretary. “Since the majority of students (more than 93%) are fully vaccinated, most schools benefit from robust community immunity that serves as a powerful shield against the virus,” Nojiri said. “To further empower families and maintain transparency, the department recently published a first-of-its-kind online school-level vaccination data tool so parents can make informed health and educational decisions.” Nearly 1,000 school nurses in Pennsylvania also attended in-person and live virtual medical briefings the department hosted this summer to help healthcare providers identify and treat patients with measles, she said. Pennsylvania’s secretaries of health and education have written multiple letters to all Pennsylvania schools about the importance of vaccine requirements for children attending school to help increase immunization reporting and reduce vaccine-preventable diseases, she said. These letters also reminded school leaders of their responsibility under the law to submit vaccine data to the department by Dec. 31 every year. The departments are partnering with non-reporting schools to achieve higher rates of reporting, while collaborating with local healthcare providers to expand access to routine immunization across the state, she said. Measles symptoms usually start seven to 14 days after contact with the virus, according to the Mayo Clinic. The illness begins with a high fever, dry cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by tiny white spots inside the mouth and a distinct red rash that spreads downward from the face. Local hospitals urge anyone who is unvaccinated, or whose children have not been vaccinated, to get the MMR vaccine as soon as possible, since measles can cause serious health complications in the near- and long-term. Babies, children and those with underlying health problems are especially vulnerable. Also at risk are those who cannot be vaccinated because they are undergoing cancer treatments or have other health issues. One in 5 who acquire the virus require hospitalization, and some who get it when they’re young have lifelong complications, health officials said. news.content_zh: 宾夕法尼亚州斯库尔基尔县的学校正在为学生可能出现的麻疹病例做准备,这是该州确认该县近二十年来首例麻疹病例后采取的措施。该病毒与该州近期麻疹病例的上升有关,2026年报告了835例病例,且当周病例增加了129例。自8月下旬以来,已发生四例与麻疹相关的死亡,这是近35年来首次出现死亡病例。尽管美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)未将这四例死亡纳入其全国统计,但州官员强调了疫苗接种的重要性,指出该县超过93%的学生已完成疫苗接种。学校管理人员已制定了应对疑似病例的程序,包括隔离有症状的学生并与州卫生部门协调。学校护士接受过识别症状、隔离学生以及通知公共卫生官员的培训。州政府还发布了一个在线工具,供家长查看学校层面的疫苗接种数据,并为医疗保健提供者提供了识别和治疗麻疹病例的指导。官员敦促家长确保其子女的MMR 疫苗接种疫苗接种情况最新,并让生病的孩子留在家中,因为麻疹具有高度传染性,且在皮疹出现前即可传播。

news.content_title: World Cup travel and low vaccination fuel Latin American measles outbreaks
news.content: Countries in Latin America are being urged to strengthen vaccination and surveillance to fight measles as the region records the highest number of cases in more than two decades, disease experts say. Low levels of vaccination coupled with travel during the FIFA World Cup have fuelled the resurgence of the highly contagious disease, which spreads easily through the air and mostly affects children. Measles is preventable through vaccination but immunization coverage for the disease in the Americas is below the level needed to protect the population. So far in 2026 the Americas have recorded the highest number of confirmed measles cases in the last 22 years, according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional office of the World Health Organization. Between January and August, more than 51,000 cases of the disease were reported, almost triple the number recorded during all of 2025, when 15,152 confirmed cases were reported and the region lost its measles-free status. In an August advisory, PAHO urged countries in the region to strengthen vaccination, epidemiological surveillance and rapid response to measles outbreaks because the public health risk associated with the disease was “very high”. Daniel Salas, executive manager of the special programme for comprehensive immunization at PAHO, told SciDev.Net: “Measles leaves no room for complacency. Each outbreak highlights immunity gaps that must be addressed urgently.” World Cup fever Case numbers are particularly high in Guatemala, Mexico, the United States, and Peru, which together, account for 95 per cent of all cases registered in the Americas so far this year, according to PAHO. The US has reported 39 new outbreaks so far this year and 3,471 confirmed cases up to mid-September, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in an update last week (18 September). Public health experts say the resurgence of the disease is being driven largely by declining vaccination rates, compounded by the high volume of people traveling across the region for the June-July World Cup, held in Mexico, the US, and Canada. Bianca de Oliveira Cata Preta, a professor in the department of public health at the Federal University of Paraná, Brazil, told SciDev.Net: “The combination of these factors is what seems to have favored the spread of the virus, giving rise to the scenario we have now.” Measles is the most contagious disease affecting humans. It is estimated that one infected person can infect 12 to 18 other people, The high mobility associated with international travel and mass events are factors that can favor the spread of the virus within and between countries.” Bianca de Oliveira Cata Preta, professor, department of public health, Federal University of Paraná, Brazil Industry Focus eBook - Clinical & Point of Care Diagnostics (1st edition) eBook In our latest Clinical & Point-of-Care Diagnostics Editorial eBook, we’ve brought together expert insights, emerging research, and application-focused articles. Download the latest edition PAHO says it is closely monitoring the situation in all countries with sustained measles transmission, supporting affected countries to strengthen surveillance, detect and respond quickly to cases, and close gaps in vaccine coverage. Low vaccination cover Of the measles cases registered in the Americas this year, almost three quarters (73 per cent) were people not vaccinated against the measles virus, according to the PAHO report. For most of the remaining cases, information on vaccination status was unknown or unavailable. The report says most countries and territories in the Americas still have suboptimal vaccination coverage of below 95 per cent, which is needed to protect the population against measles. Only 85 per cent of the regional population have received the two required doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine. There are several possible reasons to explain the drop in measles vaccination coverage, from difficulty of access to a growing rejection of vaccinations and lack of awareness of the risks associated with the disease, believes Cata Preta. “It is important to understand the reasons behind the low vaccination rates in each country in order to then think about strategies to combat the low coverage,” she said. Measles is transmitted through the air or by respiratory droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. It can cause high fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a rash. In some cases, it can also lead to complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness, and can be fatal. Herd immunity Renato Kfouri, vice president of the Brazilian Society of Vaccination and a paediatric infectious disease specialist, told SciDev.Net: “Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the disease and stop its spread. “International health authorities recommend that at least 95 per cent of the population be vaccinated to prevent transmission.” This is the percentage required to achieve so-called “herd immunity”, when a large percentage of the population becomes immune, making it difficult for a disease to spread. Kfouri believes the case of Brazil illustrates the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage rates. The country registered 15 cases of measles in the first 28 weeks of 2026, all of them imported. This is to be expected, according to Kfouri. But he added: “People travel and can return to the country infected, but the important thing is that these cases, even if they generated secondary cases, were controlled before they could cause outbreaks of the disease.” Maintaining high vaccination coverage and active surveillance for the early recognition of imported cases is essential, stresses Kfouri, especially when the epidemiological situation in neighboring countries deteriorates

Pa. reports 4, amid 835 cases TribLive TribLive Thu, Sep 24, 2026 • 09:26 AM Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Send SMS WhatsApp Reddit Like The measles virus is seen on an infant’s foot. (Adobe Stock) The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed 835 measles cases across 39 counties this week, marking the latest update in an outbreak that began in late April. Four deaths and 164 hospitalizations have been associated with measles this year, state health officials said. Pennsylvania has the worst measles outbreak in the U.S. this year and is the only state that’s reported deaths — four of them, the most in the country in a single year at least three decades. Those who died were two Lancaster County infants, too young to be vaccinated, in August; a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County; and an 18-year-old man in Mifflin County. The adults, unvaccinated, died in this month. Independent coroners in Pennsylvania and the state’s department of health determined the deaths were associated with having measles. As of a week ago, the federal government hadn’t acknowledged or counted those deaths on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website. Today, the CDC website lists one measles death, with no details as is typical. The site has a note accompanying the number of measles deaths: “This number is subject to change; CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed. “CDC is also working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) to develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles. This work is intended to promote consistent classification and reporting of measles deaths across jurisdictions.” On CNN recently, Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro blamed U.S. Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy for contributing to lower vaccination rates and for telling staff not to count Pennsylvania’s deaths. Shapiro and Kennedy have sparred over vaccines, including among the Amish. Lancaster County, which has a large Amish population, has the highest number of reported measles cases in the state this year: 342. Kennedy, a longtime vaccine skeptic, said he told Shapiro in a phone call that certain Americans had religious objections to the MMR vaccine because it contains cells from fetal tissue, a claim that has been debunked by the American Academy of Pediatrics. Vaccinations Healthcare providers across Pennsylvania have responded to the outbreak with a notable increase in vaccination activity. During the first three weeks of September, providers administered more than 38,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. By comparison, providers typically administer about 25,000 doses in an entire month. In August, that number jumped to more than 49,000 doses. The MMR vaccine provides 97% lifetime protection after two doses. People with two documented doses do not need additional vaccination, but those with only one dose or no vaccination records should consult a healthcare provider or pharmacist. People can get vaccinated through healthcare providers, county or municipal health departments, state health centers, federally qualified health centers or the Vaccines for Children program. Spread and symptoms Measles spreads through breathing, coughing or sneezing, and the virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms appear seven to 21 days after exposure and begin with fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A rash then develops on the head and spreads downward. Nearly 20% of people who contract measles require hospitalization. Death from measles occurs in one to three patients per 1,000 cases. People who believe they were exposed and are experiencing symptoms should contact their healthcare provider or call 877-PA-HEALTH. elements_en.time: The outbreak began in late April 2026, with the latest update on September 24, 2026. The deaths occurred in August and September 2026.
elements_en.location_and_population: The outbreak is centered in Pennsylvania, specifically affecting 39 counties. Lancaster County, with a large Amish population, has the highest number of reported cases.
elements_en.event: The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed 835 measles cases and four deaths associated with the measles virus. The deaths were attributed to measles, with two infants in Lancaster County, a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County, and an 18-year-old man in Mifflin County.
elements_en.scale_impact_and_risk: There have been 835 measles cases, 4 deaths, and 164 hospitalizations in Pennsylvania this year. The measles virus has a mortality rate of 1-3 per 1,000 cases, and nearly 20% of cases require hospitalization.
elements_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC has acknowledged one measles death, but the full details are not yet available. The CDC is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized case definition for measles deaths. Healthcare providers have increased vaccination activity, administering over 38,000 doses in the first three weeks of September 2026.

news.title_zh: 联邦政府承认1例美国麻疹死亡。宾州报告4例,伴随835例病例 - TribLIVE.com
news.source_body_en: The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 835 measles cases across 39 counties as of September 24, 2026, marking the worst outbreak in the U.S. Four deaths were associated with the measles virus, including two infants in Lancaster County, a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County, and an 18-year-old man in Mifflin County. These deaths were confirmed by independent coroners and state health officials. The federal government acknowledged one measles death on the CDC website, though details remain limited. The CDC is working on a standardized case definition for measles deaths. The outbreak has prompted increased vaccination efforts, with over 38,000 doses administered in the first three weeks of September 2026. The measles virus spreads through respiratory droplets and remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash. Nearly 20% of cases require hospitalization, and the mortality rate is 1-3 per 1,000 cases. The outbreak has raised concerns about vaccination rates, particularly among the Amish community, where religious objections to the MMR vaccine have been cited as a factor.
news.content_zh: 宾夕法尼亚州卫生部门于2026年9月24日报告称,该州39个县共有835例麻疹病例,标志着美国境内最严重的暴发疫情。与麻疹病毒相关的死亡病例共有4例,包括两例婴儿在兰开斯特县,一位40岁的女性在杰斐逊县,以及一位18岁的男性在米夫林县。这些死亡病例已由独立验尸官和州卫生官员确认。联邦政府在CDC网站上承认了一例麻疹死亡,但细节仍有限。CDC正在制定一个标准化的麻疹死亡病例定义。暴发疫情促使了增加的疫苗接种防控措施,2026年9月前三周已接种超过38,000剂疫苗。麻疹病毒通过呼吸道飞沫传播,并且在空气中和物体表面可保持感染性长达两小时。症状包括发烧、咳嗽、流鼻涕和红肿、流泪的眼睛,随后出现皮疹。近20%的病例需要住院治疗,死亡率的死亡率是每1,000例病例1-3例。暴发疫情引发了对疫苗接种死亡率的担忧,特别是在阿米什社区,宗教上对MMR疫苗的反对被列为影响因素之一。

supplementary_news.content: 0 of 2 minutes, 20 seconds Volume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard Shortcuts Play/Pause SPACE Increase Volume ↑ Decrease Volume ↓ Seek Forward → Seek Backward ← Captions On/Off c Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreen f Mute/Unmute m Decrease Caption Size - Increase Caption Size + or = Seek % 0-9 Live 00:01 02:18 02:20 Pennsylvania reports fourth death linked to measles 02:20 Get more news on Sept. 23, 2026, 10:02 PM UTC By Erika Edwards The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention acknowledged Wednesday that one measles death has occurred so far in 2026 but provided no clarity about who died or where. The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. On Wednesday, the CDC’s measles outbreak page was updated to show one death with a note that the number “is subject to change” and that the agency will “update its reporting as additional information becomes available.” The change left more questions than answers. The CDC declined to provide details about which death it was referring to or whether it occurred in Pennsylvania. The agency said its National Center for Health Statistics had verified that the death now posted on the CDC website had occurred and that measles had been listed as an underlying cause of death. Two of the people whose deaths health officials reported in Pennsylvania were babies, including a newborn whose mother had measles while she was pregnant. One was a 40-year-old woman who had a history of asthma and severe lung disease, and another was an 18-year-old who developed a rare neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. A Pennsylvania Health Department spokesperson said the department did not know which death the CDC was citing. Pennsylvania’s Health Department considers a death to be “measles associated” if the person died within 30 days of showing symptoms and testing positive for the virus. It can also take into account people’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The CDC’s website says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to “develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.” As of Wednesday, the CDC had confirmed 3,471 measles cases in 45 states and Washington, D.C., this year. More than 300 people have been hospitalized because of measles infection. Three people died of measles in 2025: an adult in New Mexico and two young girls in Texas. The CDC readily acknowledged those deaths at the time based on information from state health departments. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Health Department reported that its measles case count has soared to 835, with 111 cases in the last seven days. Two-thirds of those cases are in adults, and 164 people have been hospitalized in the state. Nearly all people who have been diagnosed with measles are unvaccinated. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are typically given around ages 1 and 5 and offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life. During measles outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old can receive booster doses

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Quick takes: Typhus outbreak in LA, measles exposure at Philly airport, Legionnaires’ in Chicago News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Measles Legionella Typhoid Share Copied to clipboard The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health is investigating a localized outbreak of flea-borne typhus in the Wilshire Center neighborhood of Los Angeles, the department said yesterday in a press release. Rates of the disease have increased in the city in recent years, with a total of 220 cases documented last year, a record high. The current outbreak includes seven symptomatic case-patients, six of whom were hospitalized. So far this year the county has tracked 109 cases. “As flea-borne typhus cases continue to increase across Los Angeles County, preventing exposure to fleas on free roaming animals and wildlife is more important than ever,” said Muntu Davis, MD, MPH, Los Angeles County Health Officer. “Community members can help protect themselves and their neighbors by keeping pets on flea control year-round, rodent proofing their homes and making sure wildlife cannot live in or around their homes. Simple steps can prevent serious illness.” Last week there were two possible measles exposures at Philadelphia International Airport. The exposures come on the heels of a reported exposure last week at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and highlight high virus activity in the state with the nation’s largest measles outbreak. Today the state will likely top 800 cases, with roughly 100 new cases reported each week, and four measles-associated deaths reported this year. The Hilton Garden Inn North Shore/Evanston, near Chicago, has been linked to two recent Legionnaires’ disease cases in visitors who reported using the hotel’s hot tub and pool during their stay. The case-patients stayed at the hotel in August, and the hotels pools and hot tubs have been closed since early September. “The Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) conducted water sampling and an environmental investigation of the hotel on September 8, 2026,” Evanston city officials said in a statement. “Both confirmed cases reported being in the pool and hot tub areas in August 2026, and those areas have been closed since September 2, 2026.” Water samples from other areas of the hotel did not detect Legionella bacteria, the statement said. Measles outbreak in Chicago shelter cost nearly $9 million, CDC estimates News brief Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Measles Federal Register / Flickr cc In JAMA Network Open yesterday, scientists from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Illinois public health agencies estimated the cost of a 2024 measles outbreak in two Chicago shelters for unhoused people newly arrived in the country at $8.7 million. The economic evaluation tallied the costs of the outbreak, which took place from March 7 to April 30, in terms of the public-health response, direct medical expenses, and productivity losses in patients in isolation or quarantine and those caring for children who missed school or daycare due to isolation. “Measles outbreak responses are highly intensive, requiring rapid case identification and isolation and contact management,” the authors wrote. Cost per infection approached $153,000 In total, 57 people, including 30 women (median age, 3 years) contracted measles amid the outbreak, and authorities traced 3,569 contacts (median age, 17 years). The estimated societal cost was $8.7 million, or $152,636 per measles case. Public-health response costs totaled $1.8 million in personnel costs, $1.4 million in vaccination expenses, $200,489 for lab testing costs, $104,263 for transportation, and $63,023 in other material costs. Though the outbreak placed a considerable cost burden on both public health and health care systems, rapid disease identification and mass vaccination among shelter residents prevented a more costly and larger outbreak. Direct medical costs tallied $4.4 million, mostly from hospitalizations, and estimated productivity losses were $683,895, with 17,113 lost school days. Total health-sector and payer costs, including public health response and direct medical costs, were $8 million ($140,638 per case, and $2,246 per shelter contact). “This outbreak response was one of the most expensive in the measles postelimination era due to the large costs associated with vaccination and isolation and quarantine in hospitals,” the authors wrote. “Though the outbreak placed a considerable cost burden on both public health and health care systems, rapid disease identification and mass vaccination among shelter residents prevented a more costly and larger outbreak.” “Strategies to reduce disease transmission and costs during outbreaks among undervaccinated populations living in congregate settings may include funding non–health care isolation and quarantine spaces and vaccinating new shelter residents on arrival,” the researchers concluded. Ebola outbreak in DR Congo approaches 7,800 cases News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Ebola Viral Hemorrhagic Fever UNMEER / Flickr cc The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to infect those in Ituri province at an alarming rate, according to a new report published by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) yesterday. According to the report, the DRC has 7,773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 deaths, with 40 new confirmed cases and 27 deaths reported during a 48-hour period earlier this week. “Ituri province remains the most affected, with 5,966 cases, including 2,737 deaths, reported from 28 of 36 health zones,” the ECDC wrote. “In total, 84.5% of identified case contacts are under follow-up in the affected provinces.” Without a high rate of case contact follow-up, the outbreak will continue to ravage the region, experts have warned, with new, unknown transmission chains accounting for new cases. Efforts to ensure safe burials Today the World Health Organization (WHO) published an account of a family’s resistance to safe burial techniques in the DRC, with the family refusing a safe and dignified burial for more than 24 hours because they did not want a body bag used. Experts in risk communication and community engagement were called in, and eventually a safe burial took place. The WHO said acts of community engagement and education are the best tools currently used to stop this outbreak. supplementary_news.content: FILE – This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) By David Mowery | dmowery@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: September 22, 2026 at 10:15 AM EDT | UPDATED: September 22, 2026 at 12:10 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The number of reported measles cases in Pennsylvania is nearing 800, including five in Berks County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported in its latest update Monday that 792 measles cases have been confirmed across 39 counties. The department posts updates three times a week at its dashboard, pa.gov/measles . The department’s update noted the following: • New positive cases since Sept. 18: 25 • Total counties: 39 • Total cumulative cases: 792 • Total hospitalizations: 155 • Total confirmed measles-associated deaths: 4 • Measles cases among vaccinated individuals: 4 (less than 1% of cases) According to the dashboard, Lancaster County remains the leader in cases with 323. Cases in the region: Chester County, 76; Lebanon County, 21; Montgomery County, 3; Lehigh County, 2; and Schuylkill County, 1. State health officials said they have administered more than 4,800 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 148 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities since late April when the outbreak began. Overall, state health center staff have administered more than 6,900 MMR vaccine doses this year. The department reported that health care providers have seen an increased interest from people seeking MMR vaccinations. In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer about 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine. Officials said more than 46,000 MMR vaccines were given in August and more than 25,000 doses have been administered over the first two weeks of September. The department advises that the best protection against measles is to get fully vaccinated. The two-dose MMR vaccine boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection. Those who have two documented doses of MMR do not need another, the department said. Adults who have only one dose or cannot find their vaccination records should talk with a health care provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Officials said measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious short- and long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling, with nearly 20% of people who contract measles being hospitalized. Death from measles, though rare, occurs in 1 to 3 patients per 1,000 cases, they said. Measles is spread when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area, the department said. Symptoms begin with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. Without proper protection or supportive care, measles can be deadly, officials said. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. If you believe you were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms, you are advised to contact your health care provider or call the health department’s hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). supplementary_news.content: At a glance Measles cases in the Americas reach highest levels in 22 years Guatemala, Mexico, the US, Peru account for 95 per cent of confirmed cases Outbreaks fuelled by low vaccination coverage, FIFA World Cup travel Countries in Latin America are being urged to strengthen vaccination and surveillance to fight measles as the region records the highest number of cases in more than two decades, disease experts say. Low levels of vaccination coupled with travel during the FIFA World Cup have fuelled the resurgence of the highly contagious disease, which spreads easily through the air and mostly affects children. Measles is preventable through vaccination but immunisation coverage for the disease in the Americas is below the level needed to protect the population. So far in 2026 the Americas have recorded the highest number of confirmed measles cases in the last 22 years , according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional office of the World Health Organization. Measles leaves no room for complacency. Each outbreak highlights immunity gaps that must be addressed urgently. - Daniel Salas, executive manager of the special programme for comprehensive immunisation, PAHO Between January and August, more than 51,000 cases of the disease were reported , almost triple the number recorded during all of 2025, when 15,152 confirmed cases were reported and the region lost its measles-free status. In an August advisory , PAHO urged countries in the region to strengthen vaccination, epidemiological surveillance and rapid response to measles outbreaks because the public health risk associated with the disease was “very high”. Daniel Salas, executive manager of the special programme for comprehensive immunisation at PAHO, told SciDev.Net : “Measles leaves no room for complacency. Each outbreak highlights immunity gaps that must be addressed urgently.” World Cup fever Case numbers are particularly high in Guatemala, Mexico, the United States, and Peru, which together, account for 95 per cent of all cases registered in the Americas so far this year, according to PAHO . The US has reported 39 new outbreaks so far this year and 3,471 confirmed cases up to mid-September, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) said in an update last week (18 September). Public health experts say the resurgence of the disease is being driven largely by declining vaccination rates, compounded by the high volume of people traveling across the region for the June-July World Cup, held in Mexico, the US, and Canada. Bianca de Oliveira Cata Preta, a professor in the department of public health at the Federal University of Paraná, Brazil, told SciDev.Net : “The combination of these factors is what seems to have favoured the spread of the virus, giving rise to the scenario we have now.” Measles is the most contagious disease affecting humans. It is estimated that one infected person can infect 12 to 18 other people , “The high mobility associated with international travel and mass events are factors that can favour the spread of the virus within and between countries,” Cata Preta added. PAHO says it is closely monitoring the situation in all countries with sustained measles transmission, supporting affected countries to strengthen surveillance, detect and respond quickly to cases, and close gaps in vaccine coverage. Low vaccination cover Of the measles cases registered in the Americas this year, almost three quarters (73 per cent) were people not vaccinated against the measles virus, according to the PAHO report . For most of the remaining cases, information on vaccination status was unknown or unavailable. The report says most countries and territories in the Americas still have suboptimal vaccination coverage of below 95 per cent, which is needed to protect the population against measles. Only 85 per cent of the regional population have received the two required doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine. There are several possible reasons to explain the drop in measles vaccination coverage, from difficulty of access to a growing rejection of vaccinations and lack of awareness of the risks associated with the disease, believes Cata Preta. “It is important to understand the reasons behind the low vaccination rates in each country in order to then think about strategies to combat the low coverage,” she said. Measles is transmitted through the air or by respiratory droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. It can cause high fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a rash. In some cases, it can also lead to complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness, and can be fatal. Herd immunity Renato Kfouri, vice president of the Brazilian Society of Vaccination and a paediatric infectious disease specialist, told SciDev.Net : “Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the disease and stop its spread. “International health authorities recommend that at least 95 per cent of the population be vaccinated to prevent transmission.” This is the percentage required to achieve so-called “herd immunity”, when a large percentage of the population becomes immune, making it difficult for a disease to spread. Kfouri believes the case of Brazil illustrates the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage rates. The country registered 15 cases of measles in the first 28 weeks of 2026, all of them imported. This is to be expected, according to Kfouri. But he added: “People travel and can return to the country infected, but the important thing is that these cases, even if they generated secondary cases, were controlled before they could cause outbreaks of the disease.” Maintaining high vaccination coverage and active surveillance for the early recognition of imported cases is essential, stresses Kfouri, especially when the epidemiological situation in neighbouring countries deteriorates

supplementary_news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services PITTSBURGH Measles Add Topic PA measles cases jump again, but virus is still skipping Allegheny Finch Walker USA TODAY NETWORK Sept. 24, 2026, 10:58 a.m. ET Hear this story Pennsylvania has seen a rise in measles cases, with 835 confirmed cases and four deaths as of late September. The vast majority of cases, over 99%, have occurred in individuals who were not fully vaccinated. Lancaster County is the most affected area, though potential exposures have been reported at a Pittsburgh children's hospital. Weeks after Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. bickered about the Keystone State's measles reporting, measles cases throughout Pennsylvania are continuing to multiply as the end of September approaches. Cases across the commonwealth increased by more than 100 over the past week as of Sept. 23, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health's measles dashboard. Lancaster County, where two measles-associated deaths were reported in August, was still seeing the most illness, with 342 confirmed cases of measles as of Sept. 23. While no cases had been reported among Allegheny County residents, other counties in the area were seeing additional cases. Here's what to know. How many measles cases are there in Pennsylvania? There were a total of 835 confirmed cases of measles spread across Pennsylvania as of Sept. 23, with 111 new cases in the past week, according to the state dashboard. Of those cases, more than 99% occurred in people who were not fully vaccinated, with under 1% occurring in people who were fully vaccinated. A total of 164 people had been hospitalized. Does Pittsburgh have any measles cases? Pittsburgh had no confirmed measles cases as of Sept. 23. But patients at UPMC Children's Hospital were exposed to the disease multiple times in August when out-of-county individuals who were infected with the virus visited the hospital, according to the county health department. Exposures took place on Aug. 12 and Aug. 18 when a patient visited the hospital's emergency department, with additional exposures occurring on Aug. 27. On Aug. 27, multiple groups at UPMC Children's were exposed to the virus, officials said, including those in the Giraffe/Hippo Waiting Room on the third floor from 1 to 4 p.m.; the Giraffe Clinic on the third floor from 2 to 5 p.m.; the cafeteria on the 3rd floor from 3 to 5 p.m.; the main lobby on the first floor from 1 to 5 p.m.; and the Grape/Purple Elevators from 1 to 5 p.m. Here's a look at measles cases in the broader Pittsburgh area as of Sept. 23, the last day the state's measles dashboard was updated: Allegheny: 0 Armstrong: 2 Beaver: 0 Butler: 1 (diagnosed on Aug. 25 according to hospital spokesperson; not reported by state dashboard as of Sept. 23) Fayette: 0 Lawrence: 0 Washington: 0 Westmoreland: 2 Where are measles cases spreading in Pennsylvania? There's confirmed community transmission of measles in Centre, Chester, Clearfield, Indiana, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin, Snyder, Somerset, Union and York counties, according to the state department of health. How many measles deaths have there been in 2026? Pennsylvania's department of health had confirmed four measles-associated deaths across the commonwealth as of Sept. 23. Two of the individuals lived in Lancaster County, one resided in Jefferson County and the fourth was from Mifflin County, according to health department officials. The first two deaths, both infants, according to NPR, were confirmed by the state on Aug. 25. The state confirmed two more deaths on Sept. 15. The third and fourth deaths involved a 40-year-old woman with an active infection and an 18-year-old with a rare neurological complication from measles, NPR reported. None of the individuls were vaccinated. Before 2026, there had been no measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania in about 35 years, according to health department officials. How does measles spread? How contagious is it? Measles spreads through the air when a sick person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to the Centers for Disease Control. It can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after a person who is sick with the virus leaves the area. It's extremely contagious and can sicken up to nine out of 10 people who come into close contact with an infected person if they aren't protected against the virus. Unvaccinated people are most at risk of catching the disease. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine provides about 97% immunity from measles, according to the CDC. Young children typically don't get their second dose until they reach four to six years of age, leaving them with about 93% protection against the disease. Infants generally don't get their first dose until they're 12 to 15 months old. The CDC notes that infants between the ages of six and 11 months can get a dose of the vaccine if they're going to travel outside of the U.S., though they should still get two additional doses at the recommended ages to provide long-term protection. What are the symptoms of measles? Measles symptoms generally appear within seven to 14 days after coming into contact with the virus, according to the CDC, though the incubation period can last up to 21 days. Symptoms can include a high fever, cough, runny nose, red/watery eyes, white spots inside the mouth and a rash that begins on the face at the hairline and moves downward on the body. The virus can also cause numerous complications, including ear infections, diarrhea, lasting immune system damage, hospitalization, pneumonia, encephalitis, pregnancy problems and death. People who believe they were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Allegheny County residents who are worried about possible exposures should call Allegheny County Health Department at 412-687-2243. Residents throughout Pennsylvania who are concerned about potential exposures should call the Pennsylvania Department of Health’s toll-free hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH. Pennsylvanians can access the measles dashboard, current guidance and additional information at pa.gov/measles. Finch Walker is the Pittsburgh Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network.
