supplementary_news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Measles Add Topic Measles spread south in Ohio as new cases keep growing Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Sept. 24, 2026, 2:51 p.m. ET Hear this story Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with 196 cases reported across 16 counties this year. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, a surge experts attribute to declining vaccination rates. A new county is reporting measles cases as Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state had 16 new cases in the past week, a 66% decrease from the 47 new cases the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 196 cases in 16 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Sept. 24. That's up from 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17; 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10; 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3; 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27; 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20; 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13; and 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Morrow County, northeast of Columbus, joins the list with eight cases reported in the past week. And in Southwest Ohio, two people who tested positive for measles may have exposed others at Cincinnati Children's Hospital's emergency department on Sept. 14 and 15, according to the Cincinnati Health Department. ODH does not show measles cases in Hamilton County as of Sept. 24. "These patients were exposed to measles in the state in which they live and have since been discharged from Cincinnati Children’s and returned to their home state," a Sept. 17 statement from the health department said.The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Sept. 11 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 3,387 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 32 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 44 (six new cases) Harrison: 11 Holmes: 9 Knox: 5 Meigs: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 8 (eight new cases) Ottawa: 1 Portage: 1 Trumbull: 8 (one new case) Tuscarawas: 13 Wayne: 44 (one new case) The case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least four people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 23, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading in Ohio? Portage County confirmed its first measles case, the county Health District announced Sept. 8. At the time, no public exposure locations associated with this case had been identified. Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, but the state dashboard shows additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reported 34 new measles cases last week, nearly four times its nine cases the week prior. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Press shift + ◄ to open this menu Support Our Work News & Features Outdoors Sports Arts Opinion Events Daily Roundup Newsletters Glacier Park Prints Flathead Living Glacier Journal Sponsored Police Blotter Reader Poll Photos & Video Recent Publications Public Notices Podcasts About Us Advertise Contact Us Search in https://flatheadbeacon.com/ Healthcare Health Officials Identify Three Measles Exposure Sites in Flathead County Exposures occurred Sept. 8-11 at Glacier Highland in West Glacier, Logan Health Primary Care in Columbia Falls and on an eastbound Amtrak train from West Glacier By Zoë Buhrmaster September 21, 2026 The Flathead City-County Health Department on March 11, 2021. Hunter D’Antuono | Flathead Beacon A person infected with measles visited Flathead County from Sept. 8 to Sept. 11, exposing people at three known sites across the valley, health officials announced Sunday. Officials said they are awaiting test results on a suspected case and said more exposure sites may be identified. The Flathead City-County Health Department confirmed two measles cases in residents last year, when Montana saw its first measles outbreak in 35 years. The county has expanded resources for people with questions about the disease, including an online self-assessment tool and a prerecorded measles information phone line. Known exposure sites and dates include: Glacier Highland Gift Store & Restaurant in West Glacier, Sept. 8 to 11 Logan Health Primary Care in Columbia Falls, Sept. 8 between noon and 5 p.m. Amtrak Train 8, eastbound from West Glacier on Sept. 11 Anyone who may have been exposed during those timeframes should monitor for symptoms for 21 days and complete the county’s online self-assessment form, which can be found here. When an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, they release tiny droplets containing the measles virus. The virus can linger in the air up for to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. It can also spread when a person touches contaminated surface and then touches their mouth, eyes or nose. Initial symptoms usually include a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, along with small white spots inside the cheeks. A red rash typically appears on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Health officials urge anyone who develops symptoms to call their health care provider immediately. People who believe they may have measles should stay home and avoid visitors until they are no longer contagious or measles has been ruled out. People who are immune through vaccination, lab-confirmed immunity or prior infection, as well as those born before 1957, are generally not considered at risk. Officials said about 90% of unvaccinated people who are exposed will become infected. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is about 97% effective after two doses and is the best protection against the disease. Self-assessment tools, the measles phone line and other resources are available on the county’s measles website, where confirmed cases and exposure locations will be posted. zoe@flatheadbeacon.com

Health ‘We’re literally seeing new forms of measles’: Infectious disease doc warns about scary Pennsylvania development By McKenzie Beard Published Sep. 23, 2026, 11:12 a.m. ET 6262 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak has taken a disturbing turn. The highly contagious disease has ripped through communities across the Keystone State in recent months, sickening hundreds, sending scores to the hospital and claiming four lives. Now, as the virus continues to spread, doctors are seeing it turn up in patients they rarely encountered before — and learning how to treat them in real time. 3 US measles cases in 2026 have already surpassed last year’s total, which was the highest tally in more than 30 years. weerapat1003 – stock.adobe.com Enter: Congenital measles, a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a mother who is infected around the time of delivery passes the virus onto her baby in the womb or during birth. For much of history, cases like these were rare. Before vaccines, most people were infected with measles during childhood, so women typically had lasting natural immunity by the time they had children of their own. Later, widespread vaccination provided that same protection without requiring people to contract the disease. But measles, once declared eliminated in the US, is making a comeback nationwide as vaccination rates decline and fewer young adults have natural immunity from prior infection. “Because of this, we’re literally seeing new forms of measles,” Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, told The Guardian. “We don’t have a lot of information about what happens with it.” Just last month, a woman with measles in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, delivered a stillborn baby who died from a ruptured spleen in a case the coroner classified as a measles-associated death. The midwife who attended the birth told the mother that the baby’s death was linked to her severe case of measles and lack of vaccination, according to The Atlantic. 3 Women who contract measles during pregnancy can pass the virus onto their newborn in the womb or during delivery. pressmaster – stock.adobe.com Measles during pregnancy can increase the risk of pregnancy loss, premature delivery and low birth weight. Up to 30% of babies whose mothers are infected around the time of delivery may also contract the virus, putting them at risk for serious illness. “Congenital measles typically presents in the newborn with fever and rash within the first 10 days of life, and can occasionally cause severe complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis and even death,” Dr. Manish Trivedi, head of infectious diseases at AtlantiCare, told The Post. The trouble may not end there. Congenital measles also increases the risk of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, a rare and progressive neurological disorder that causes widespread inflammation and scarring in the brain. It is almost always fatal and has no cure. Adding to the concern is that few pediatricians across the country have experience treating newborns infected with the virus. Earlier this month, the American Academy of Pediatrics published an FAQ on congenital measles to help address that knowledge gap, laying out guidance on preventing, diagnosing and treating the infection in newborns whose mothers have measles. And this isn’t just a theoretical concern. “If measles keeps spreading, we’re going to see more pregnant women exposed to the virus,” Trivedi said. As of Sept. 18, 3,471 confirmed measles cases had been reported across the US in 2026, according to the latest federal data, spanning 39 outbreaks. 3 Newborns are at an increased risk for severe disease from a measles infection. andriano_cz – stock.adobe.com With more than three months still left in the year, that has already surpassed 2025’s total of 2,289 confirmed cases — the highest annual tally in more than three decades. But Trivedi stressed that not all pregnant women are in immediate danger. “Pregnant women are considered at higher risk for complications from measles, but those who already have evidence of immunity are generally well protected,” he said. “The greatest concern is for pregnant women who are not immune and become exposed or infected.” Trivedi recommends that pregnant women check their vaccination history or immunity with their health care provider, especially if they’ve been exposed to measles or live in or travel to an area with an outbreak. 62 What do you think? Post a comment. The catch: The MMR vaccine contains a live, weakened version of the measles virus and can’t be given during pregnancy. “Women who are not immune should be vaccinated before pregnancy or after delivery,” Trivedi said. “If a nonimmune pregnant woman is exposed to measles, she should contact her healthcare provider immediately because intravenous immune globulin can be given within six days of exposure to reduce the risk or severity of infection,” he advised. supplementary_news.content: Local Sports High School Huddle Scene Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH What to know about measles in NC with Pennsylvania outbreak announced Iris Seaton Asheville Citizen Times Sept. 23, 2026, 12:34 p.m. ET Pennsylvania has confirmed 25 new measles cases, bringing its total to 792 for the year. Nationwide, measles cases have significantly increased, with several states reporting over 100 cases this year. Symptoms of measles include high fever, cough, runny nose, and a characteristic red, blotchy rash. An outbreak of measles has been announced in Pennsylvania, with 25 new positive cases confirmed since Sept. 18. Nationwide, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that measles cases have increased significantly over the past several years, by hundreds of cases in some cases, including those of Pennsylvania and Utah. As previously reported by the Citizen Times, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced Aug. 31 that a case of measles could have spread to residents of Buncombe County via a sick traveler. The Pennsylvania Department of Health continues to provide up-to-date information on measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths on its measles dashboard at pa.gov/measles. Here's what we know about the outbreak so far, plus information on NC's cases and more. Pennsylvania measles outbreak: What we know The Pennsylvania Department of Health announced an outbreak of measles in the state on Sept. 21. The notice confirmed 792 measles cases across 39 counties in the state so far this year, including 25 new positive cases since Sept. 18, 2026. Latest measles exposure in Buncombe County The latest measles news in Buncombe County happened in August due to a sick traveler, with possible exposure locations including: Exxon, 1920 Four Seasons Blvd., Hendersonville, on Aug. 25 from 9:30-11:45 a.m. - Monitor for symptoms until Sept. 15 Holiday Inn Express, 435 Smokey Park Highway, Asheville, on Aug. 26 from 1-10:30 a.m. - Monitor for symptoms until Sept. 16 Is there measles in North Carolina? How many measles cases are there in NC? The N.C. DHHS says 24 measles cases were identified in the state between December 2025 and February 2026. This includes 17 cases in patients under 18 and five in patients over 18. Of these patients, 68% were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. These numbers do not include measles cases reported in travelers to North Carolina. No further measles cases have been reported in the state since February. How many people are vaccinated against measles in North Carolina? According to the CDC, roughly 93.7% of N.C. kindergarteners were vaccinated for the 2025-2026 school year. This is down slightly from 94.2% in the 2024-2025 school year. Which states have the most measles cases? According to CDC data updated Sept. 18, states with 100 or more cases of measles recorded in 2026 so far include: Pennsylvania - 745 South Carolina - 670 Utah - 527 Texas - 192 Virginia - 178 Wisconsin - 158 Florida - 147 Ohio - 124 Arizona - 110 What are the symptoms of measles? What does a measles rash look like? Symptoms of measles usually begin 7-14 days after exposure, but can appear up to 21 days later. Measles symptoms may include: High fever, potentially exceeding 104 degrees Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Tiny white spots on the inner cheeks, gums, and roof of the mouth appear two to three days after symptoms begin A rash that is red, raised, and blotchy, usually starting on the face and spreading to the trunk, arms, and legs, three to five days after symptoms begin Can measles be deadly? Harvard Health explains that complications of measles are most common among children under the age of five, adults over the age of 20, pregnant women, and people with impaired immune systems. Measles is fatal in up to three out of 1,000 cases. In 2025, the CDC reported that three people died in the U.S. of measles among the 1,912 cases reported. How does measles spread? The state health department website states that the measles virus lives in the nose and throat. It spreads when someone with measles talks, sneezes, or coughs, releasing tiny droplets containing the virus into the air. Droplets can remain airborne and contaminate surfaces for up to two hours. County; officials not alarmed St. Louis Public Radio | By Sarah Fentem Published Sept. 23, 2026 at 5:00 a.m. CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Chuck Gomez / Amtrak Three cases of measles in Missouri are tied to an Amtrak train trip to Chicago. A person with measles who visited several public spaces in the St. Louis region earlier this month is connected to an Amtrak train trip associated with other cases, public health officials confirmed. The Franklin County resident is the third confirmed case of measles tied to the train journey. A person infected with measles on Aug. 27 boarded the train in Sedalia. Later, a St. Louis County resident, who was vaccinated, tested positive for the virus. On Monday, the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services released a list of places the infected person from Franklin County visited during the weekend of Sept. 12, which included several restaurants in St. Louis and St. Louis and Franklin counties in addition to a Cardinals game at Busch Stadium. St. Louis County Department of Public Health Director Kanika Cunningham said Tuesday that health officials are not treating the cases as cause for alarm. “There are some pockets of individuals who you know are unvaccinated, but right now we're not seeing this as an outbreak,” she said. “We're monitoring every day.” Franklin County Health Director Tony Buel said that he had so far not heard of the resident spreading the disease to anyone else. “I don’t believe that the person who was in Franklin County at the locations of concern has spread it to anybody,” he said. “[There’s] no confirmation of that anywhere or even any suspected cases. But keep in mind onset can be as long as 21 days.” Missouri has so far logged 10 cases of the highly contagious virus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after exposure, though they can appear up to 21 days afterward. Early symptoms include fever, runny nose, cough and red or watery eyes, followed by the characteristic measles rash. It’s particularly dangerous for very young or very old people. The United States this year has seen more measles cases than it has in decades. Close to 3,500 people have been confirmed infected so far in 2026, about 1,000 more than in the entirety of 2025. According to the CDC, 13% of children under 5 years old with reported infections have been hospitalized. As measles cases rise around the country, it’s going to be more common to see cases pop up in Missouri and St. Louis, said Nathan Koffarnus, assistant communicable disease chief at the state’s health department. “There is actually more measles circulating in our country than has been common in decades,” he said. “And so it is important to be aware of that and to be concerned.” The infected person was in several situations with prolonged, close contact, Koffarnus said. That means more people may be infected. “Those cars can be pretty full, and people are in close quarters for a prolonged period of time,” he said. “Where the exposure took place is particularly challenging. When we have these, you know, subsequent cases that were also out in the community, visited a lot of places, there's certainly a lot of opportunities for exposure to others at those spots.” Both Cunningham and Koffarnus said the best protection is the two-shot measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination, which is 97% effective. Even if people who are vaccinated get a “breakthrough” case, they said, it’s likely to be less severe than an unvaccinated person would experience. The measles vaccine, for the most part, does not wane in power. A person who receives the full series of shots likely does not need to worry about getting a booster or another dose. “I think right now the messaging is we need to raise awareness,” Cunningham said. “If you were at these places, check your vaccination status. If you're unvaccinated, quarantine, call your doctor, let them know, monitor for symptoms.” Have a question or comment about this story? Email St. Louis Public Radio. Got a news tip? Washington-Watch > Washington Watch CDC, Epidemiologists Work on Definition for Measles Deaths — Standard workgroup process began over the summer by Kristina Fiore, Director of Enterprise & Investigative Reporting, MedPage Today September 22, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday The CDC is indeed working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) on a definition for measles deaths, but the initiative was launched earlier this year and it was not at the request of the CDC. That's according to CSTE spokesperson Amy Heldman, MPH, who explained that a CSTE workgroup was launched earlier this summer "to develop future guidance to inform measles epidemiology case investigations associated with deaths." "The workgroup will work collaboratively with CSTE leadership and CDC to apply CSTE's consensus-building processes to develop a standardized case definition related to measles deaths," Heldman said in an email to MedPage Today. Convening the workgroup was part of an established and longstanding consensus-building process, not something requested by CDC, she added. CSTE hosts a number of workgroups with CDC, and this is standard practice based on the needs of jurisdictions, she said. "Determining how diseases and conditions are monitored and investigated and how data are shared at the national level is a rigorous, collaborative process involving CDC, state, tribal, local, and territorial applied epidemiologists, and other partners," Heldman said. "It is CSTE's role to convene applied epidemiologists in states and territories to reach consensus and develop guidance, criteria, and resources for public health surveillance activities." Working on a new definition for measles deaths raised eyebrows because of the way it was announced. Earlier this month, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD, altered public reporting of measles deathsopens in a new tab or window on the CDC website at the request of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The CDC's website initially listed the two measles-associated deaths recorded by Pennsylvania, but Kennedy asked Schwartz to remove them. In place of the number appeared an asterisk, which remains on the site todayopens in a new tab or window. That asterisk section includes a note that CDC is working with CSTE to "develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles." The section also says that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) "does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause" -- which confused expertsopens in a new tab or window because NCHS is not intended for outbreak data. Instead, the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System has historically been used to track outbreaks by collecting state data. "Typically, the CDC goes with whatever the state reports," said one CDC source familiar with the process who did not want to be named. "It's almost like the CDC wants to make it more difficult to count confirmed deaths," the source said. "I suppose Kennedy wants the definition to be as restrictive as possible so that it appears practically no one is dying from measles." Pennsylvania currently reports four measles-associated deathsopens in a new tab or window. It reported 97 cases in the past 7 days, and a total of 792 cases in 2026, making it one of the hardest-hit states during a measles resurgence that began in 2025. Other states that have been hit particularly hardopens in a new tab or window include Texas, South Carolina, and Utah. Last year, Texas had three measles-associated deaths. supplementary_news.content: Search | RU | EN | KG | Home News Local newsEconomyIncidentsExclusiveHealthSportsEcology About Kyrgyzstan Weather Advertising on the Website Weather Home News Local newsEconomyIncidentsExclusiveHealthSportsEcology About Kyrgyzstan For Tourists Home » News » Local news » In Bishkek, they discuss how to prevent new outbreaks of measles in Central Asia In Bishkek, they discuss how to prevent new outbreaks of measles in Central Asia Евгения Комарова • 25.09.2026, 13:13 • Local news Подробнее Переводчик с русского Аналитика событий Люди и общество Read on Telegram Read on Facebook In Bishkek, a subregional strategic dialogue titled "Immunization in Central Asia: from outbreak response to sustainable protection" has begun. Within the framework of the event, representatives from Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan are discussing ways to increase vaccination coverage and the need to transition from merely responding to outbreaks of infections to their prevention. Also participating in the discussion are representatives from UNICEF and the European Regional Office of the World Health Organization. The dialogue is organized by the Ministry of Health of Kyrgyzstan in collaboration with the UNICEF Country Office in the country and the UNICEF Centre of Excellence. Deputy Minister of Health Gulbara Ishenapysova emphasized that high population mobility, labor migration, and active trade and transport links create common risks for the spread of infectious diseases in the region. She noted that "high and sustainable vaccination coverage is not only a national task but also a common challenge for our subregion." According to the deputy minister, recent cases of measles underline the importance of timely identification of gaps in immunization to prevent new outbreaks. During the meeting, participants are addressing issues of sustainable financing for immunization programs, digitization of processes, improving data quality, epidemiological surveillance, introduction of new vaccines, and cooperation between countries. Kyrgyzstan plans to share its experience in the digitization of the immunization system and the development of information systems, while other countries in the region will present practices for using data to improve policy and epidemiological surveillance. UNICEF representative in Kyrgyzstan Samman Tapa noted that long-term investments in training healthcare workers, cold chain logistics, and information systems are essential for protecting children. Particular attention is being paid to the issues of insufficient vaccination coverage and identifying populations that have not been vaccinated. As a result of the dialogue, participants plan to outline further steps for financing immunization programs, data sharing, and strengthening cooperation in Central Asia. Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Chicago/ Crime & Emergencies Chicago Measles Alerts Spread From Union Station To Chinatown Hotel By Jo Marquez Published on September 25, 2026 SpringHill Suites Chicago Chinatown — Additional Measles Exposure Location Google Street View Chicago's measles scare just got bigger. Along with warning commuters about three separate exposure windows at Union Station, city health officials have listed a Chinatown hotel among the places where a person with a confirmed case of the highly contagious virus may have exposed others. The Chicago Department of Public Health flagged the SpringHill Suites at 2357 S. Wentworth Ave. as a public exposure site tied to a domestic traveler who was there from 10:45 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 12 through 3:40 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 13, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. The department also warned, in a notice first reported by CBS Chicago, that commuters passing through Union Station at 255 S. Canal St. may have been exposed on three separate occasions: between 10:25 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. on Sept. 10, between 8:45 p.m. and midnight on Sept. 12, and between 1:40 p.m. and 9 p.m. on Sept. 13. The hotel exposure window overlaps with some of the Union Station windows. Union Station also appeared on an exposure list earlier this year — one potential exposure was reported there after 8 p.m. on Aug. 27 and on Aug. 28, per the same CBS Chicago report. Why a Two-Hour-Old Room Can Still Be Dangerous Measles is notoriously persistent in the air. According to guidance on measles from the Chicago Department of Public Health measles facts page, the virus can remain airborne and infectious in an enclosed space for up to two hours after an infected person has left, and up to 90% of non-immune people who are exposed will go on to contract it. That combination of lingering infectiousness and near-total transmission risk among the unvaccinated is why health officials move quickly whenever a confirmed case surfaces in a high-traffic public space. Union Station itself is about as high-traffic as it gets. The terminal serves more than 3 million Amtrak passengers and 35 million Metra commuter rail riders annually across more than 300 trains a day, according to Chicago Union Station. That volume means even a narrow exposure window, like the 7-hour-20-minute Sunday afternoon alert, could theoretically have put thousands of travelers at risk. Anyone who was in either location during the listed windows should watch for measles symptoms, which the CBS Chicago report notes include rash, high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. Those symptoms can take seven to 21 days to appear after exposure, and health officials say anyone who develops them should call ahead before showing up at a doctor's office or emergency room, rather than walking in and risking further spread. The MMR vaccine is available at no cost to all Chicago residents, including through CDPH immunization clinics. Illinois Cases Already Outpace All of Last Year The exposure warnings land amid a broader statewide surge. The Illinois Department of Public Health reported 22 confirmed measles cases statewide in 2026 as of Sept. 22 — already more than the 14 total cases recorded in all of 2025, though still well below the 67 cases seen in 2024. Illinois' first 2026 case was confirmed Feb. 17 in Metro East following out-of-state travel, while Chicago logged its first case of the year on June 23 in an international traveler, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. Nationally, the picture is starker still. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 3,471 confirmed measles cases and 39 outbreaks across the United States as of Sept. 17, compared with 2,289 total confirmed cases in all of 2025. The surge has been fueled in part by interconnected regional travel; a confirmed case in late August involved a passenger aboard Chicago-bound Amtrak Train 318, which prompted exposure warnings across both Missouri and Illinois transit channels, according to the St. Louis County Department of Public Health. Hoodline previously reported on St. Louis County's first case in two decades. Illinois still maintains a statewide school measles vaccination rate of 96.78%, per the Illinois Public Health Association. Chicago-Crime & Emergencies Crime & Emergencies in ... Ongoing outbreaks in Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas, and Utah have documented hundreds of cases, mostly among unvaccinated people. And while local and federal politicians debate the definitions and impact of those measles-associated deaths, health experts worry that we’re overlooking the real problem: the threat of a full-scale epidemic. Today, we talk to one of those experts – epidemiologist Michael Mina – to figure out who’s most at risk and whether there’s any way for us to turn this epidemic around. Photograph: Hannah Beier/Reuters Analysis Why the CDC is excluding measles deaths in Pennsylvania even as outbreak appears to be ‘accelerating’ Melody Schreiber Centers for Disease Control and Prevention refuses to count four measles deaths in the state though doctors are ‘seeing new forms’ of disease The US Centers of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its measles dashboard on Friday – but it’s still not counting four measles deaths in Pennsylvania, where the outbreak appears to be accelerating and cases are appearing in ways providers have never seen before. Members of Congress on Monday requested an “immediate briefing” on the decision to change how measles deaths are reported as cases continue to rise throughout the United States, reaching levels not seen in decades. A possible measles exposure was reported in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia last week. The delay in death reporting is “curious” even after the CDC switched how it counts deaths, said Debra Houry, former CDC chief medical officer. It takes one to two days for the CDC to receive updated data to the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) after states finish death investigations. “Pennsylvania concluded the investigation on the first two deaths, so CDC would have these records by now,” Houry said. Pennsylvania asks CDC for emergency help as measles outbreak spreads Read more Meanwhile, the outbreak “seems to be accelerating”, said Dr John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “And we’re seeing, actually, types of measles we’ve never seen before,” he added. Doctors are now treating congenital measles – newborns who contracted the virus in utero or at birth – which was once exceedingly rare because most pregnant people were protected by vaccines or, before immunization, surviving measles in childhood. “Because of this, we’re literally seeing new forms of measles,” Goldman said. “We don’t have a lot of information about what happens with it.” Pennsylvania has reported 731 cases, but that number is likely an undercount, he said. Frequently when patients come to the hospital with measles, they mention that others at home are sick as well – but they haven’t been tested, Goldman said. On average, one to three people for every 1,000 cases will die of measles, and one in five will be hospitalized. The current deaths and hospital admissions in Pennsylvania are “definitely not proportional to what would be expected”, Houry said, and she believes the official numbers are “very much an undercount”. Under-testing can make it challenging to do contact tracing and sick people may not realize they need to isolate – both of which can make the spread of measles more likely. Providers are preparing for more cases and more deaths. “It’s not rocket science. If we see more measles, we’ll see more deaths,” Goldman said. “I suspect that we’re not going to see a break until most people in most communities are immune either by vaccine or infection.” Typically, the CDC collects data from states, including causes of death. Death certificates are issued at the state or local level; there are no federal death certificates. But now, the agency is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to define deaths from measles. While the CDC has its own measles case definition, it has relied upon the World Health Organization’s definition of measles deaths. Until a measles death definition is created, the CDC is relying on NCHS data, which “identifies measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about why the death count was still delayed, or whether all deaths would receive a CDC definition. Before this outbreak, measles deaths were rare in America; there were none for a decade. “When there aren’t deaths, you don’t need a precise definition,” Houry said. Pennsylvania developed a definition, and the CDC could consider adopting it, she said. Erica Schwartz, the CDC director, denied in an interview that deaths were being miscounted for political reasons, pointing instead to the process of creating a definition. “If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have Covid, often that was called a Covid-related death,” Schwartz said, referencing misinformation about how Covid deaths were counted. In reality, Covid deaths were likely under-counted. Pennsylvania’s definition of “measles death” clearly excludes unrelated deaths, so the bus scenario would not apply, Houry said. “Dr Schwartz’s comments are not only not helpful, but contribute to misinformation.” But this isn’t the most important issue right now, she added. “I would focus less on the definition itself and responding to the measles outbreak, and that’s what the focus of the CDC director should be.” Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, has cast doubt on the Pennsylvania deaths and reportedly instructed Schwartz not to include them in the CDC tally. Kennedy only mentioned the measles outbreak once in a speech spanning nearly an hour and a half at an anti-vaccine conference on Thursday. He noted only that deaths from measles are headline news and he asked that severe side effects and deaths from vaccines get the same attention. About one to two people in a million experience severe side effects from vaccines, while with measles one in five people are hospitalized and one to three in 1,000 die. Pennsylvania has responded aggressively to the outbreak, standing up more than 100 pop-up clinics and requesting additional vaccination support from the CDC. The state department of health has “done a spectacular job of dealing with this”, Goldman said. Tests have a 24-hour turnaround time. “I have called them up on a Thursday before the holiday weekend and arranged for them to do testing before it closed at noon the following day,” Goldman said. “They have provided us with information, and they have provided us with really really good support.” While there is a likely undercount of cases, “it’s not because they couldn’t get a test”, he said. “It’s because they were sick at home and did not seek medical care.” The response hasn’t been limited to the health department, Houry noted. “Health systems and clinicians are really stepping up across the state to get vaccines to their communities.” Before this outbreak, Goldman was the rare American doctor who had seen measles, once in 1988 and once in 1992. Between 1992 and 2026, he didn’t see a single case. Now, “we’re seeing at least one every day”, he said. He’s preparing for three to six more months of this. “Never in my life did I think I was ever going to see measles again,” he said. He fears for other vaccine-preventable diseases: whooping cough, diphtheria, polio. “In a way, I think this is a warning,” he said. “What worries me is measles is conceivably the canary in the coal mine.” Explore more on these topics Pennsylvania US healthcare MMR Vaccines and immunisation Trump administration Health US politics analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Partner of woman killed by US hunter who allegedly mistook her for deer says death ‘no accident’ Why a supercharged El Niño is putting Hawaii in the bullseye of more storms ‘I’m 100% natural’: how Japan’s 90-year-old bodybuilder is still winning titles In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters Most viewed Most viewed

(KY3) -The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed more than 3,000 measles cases nationwide so far this year, including 10 in Missouri. “Here recently we have seen an increase in measles cases in the state of Missouri,” said Stephanie Woehl of the Springfield-Greene County Health Department. Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases known. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services published a health alert earlier this month warning residents of surging measles cases in the Midwest. The department notified the St. Louis area Monday about a third measles exposure, linked to a Chicago-bound train on Aug. 27. “We are seeing a resurgence of the measles virus because individuals who are receiving the MMR vaccine are declining,” Woehl said. Missouri’s measles vaccination rate stands at 89.5%, far below the 95% coverage level health officials recommend to prevent community outbreaks and achieve herd immunity. “The measles vaccine is very effective. It’s a two-dose series, if you get both doses in the series, 97 percent effectiveness, with one dose, 93,” Woehl said. Health experts say measles can be difficult to diagnose early because symptoms resemble a common cold. The red-brown rash associated with measles appears in later stages of infection. Woehl recommends residents take proactive steps to protect themselves. “Check your evidence of immunity now, check your vaccination records, talk to your healthcare provider. If you do not have evidence of receiving the MMR vaccine, now is a great time to get that vaccine,” Woehl said. Health officials also recommend that anyone experiencing symptoms call ahead before visiting a clinic. This allows staff to prepare and prevent exposing others in waiting rooms and public spaces. reach 30-year high following Scottsdale pharmacy exposure Close Maricopa County has reached the highest count of measles recorded in the area in three decades. By Alaina Kwan Published: Sep. 21, 2026 at 4:16 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Maricopa County health officials last week confirmed another case of measles, bringing the county’s total to 28 cases this year — the highest count recorded in the area in three decades. The Maricopa County Department of Public Health on Thursday announced the latest exposure risk stems from a Walgreens near Via Linda and Frank Lloyd Wright Boulevard in Scottsdale. Officials said an infected individual visited the pharmacy earlier this month. Public health officials advise anyone who visited the store during that window to monitor for symptoms through Sept. 29. Measles symptoms typically include a high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes, followed by a distinct rash. Local medical experts warn that the virus spreads rapidly and poses serious health risks, particularly as children return to classrooms and respiratory virus season begins. “It can linger in a room for hours, even after you leave, up to two hours,” said Dr. Frank LoVecchio, a local emergency physician. “So if I have measles and I walk into a room and I cough and it’s in the air, I leave the room and two hours later... someone else walks in the room, they can catch measles.” LoVecchio noted that declining vaccination rates over recent years have made communities more vulnerable to outbreaks. Because the virus is airborne and highly contagious, an infected person can easily spread it to 10 or 12 unvaccinated individuals in a shared space. While most children recover from the illness, health officials emphasize that measles can lead to severe complications if transmitted to higher-risk populations. “Most kids who get measles are not going to die from it,” LoVecchio said. “The problem is when they give it to older people, and when they bring it home and bring it to somebody maybe who’s not vaccinated, that older person could develop pneumonia, could develop meningitis or a brain infection. And, you know, unfortunately, they could die of that.” Physicians stress that widespread immunization remains the most effective way to halt community spread and protect vulnerable populations, including infants and immunocompromised individuals who cannot receive the vaccine. “The good news is we can prevent it, usually with vaccination, but we all need to do it,” LoVecchio said. “The great majority of it needs to be vaccinated to kind of protect everyone. If your child’s vaccinated, they’re less likely to bring it home.” The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is typically administered to children as a two-dose series, while adults without documented immunity generally require a single dose. According to LoVecchio, protective antibodies can begin developing as early as one week after the first dose. Residents seeking vaccination or those who believe they may have been exposed should contact their primary care provider before visiting a clinic or emergency department in person. (KATU) — Clark County Public Health is investigating two confirmed measles cases involving unvaccinated children, including a possible exposure at a Battle Ground school. One person who tested positive for measles was at River HomeLink, 610A SW Eaton Blvd., while contagious, health officials said. The possible exposure occurred Thursday, Sept. 17, from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Public Health is working with Battle Ground Public Schools to identify students and staff who are not protected against measles. Those people will be excluded from school, child care and other public settings for 21 days, officials said. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local Weather WE INVESTIGATE Video Newsletters Sunny 74o Watch 24/7 Trending Nick Bosa Restaurant break-ins 🎸 Dolly Parton Day ⛽ Gas prices 🛩️ Fleet Week 🎙️ Women Who Lead 🗳️ Election guide Expand Centers for Disease Control and Prevention CDC reports first measles death amid confusion over Pennsylvania cases The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. By Erika Edwards | NBC News • Published September 23, 2026 • Updated on September 23, 2026 at 5:10 pm Getty Images Computer illustration of a measles virus particle. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention acknowledged Wednesday that one measles death has occurred so far in 2026 but provided no clarity about who died or where. The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. On Wednesday, the CDC’s measles outbreak page was updated to show one death with a note that the number “is subject to change” and that the agency will “update its reporting as additional information becomes available.” Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are WATCH HERE The change left more questions than answers. The CDC declined to provide details about which death it was referring to or whether it occurred in Pennsylvania. The agency said its National Center for Health Statistics had verified that the death now posted on the CDC website had occurred and that measles had been listed as an underlying cause of death. Two of the people whose deaths health officials reported in Pennsylvania were babies, including a newborn whose mother had measles while she was pregnant. One was a 40-year-old woman who had a history of asthma and severe lung disease, and another was an 18-year-old who developed a rare neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. A Pennsylvania Health Department spokesperson said the department did not know which death the CDC was citing. Health Sep 15 Pennsylvania teen dies from measles complications, health officials report Health Sep 13 Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications, marking the state's third this year Health Aug 25 Two die of measles in Pennsylvania outbreak Pennsylvania’s Health Department considers a death to be “measles associated” if the person died within 30 days of showing symptoms and testing positive for the virus. It can also take into account people’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The CDC’s website says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to “develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.” As of Wednesday, the CDC had confirmed 3,471 measles cases in 45 states and Washington, D.C., this year. More than 300 people have been hospitalized because of measles infection. Three people died of measles in 2025: an adult in New Mexico and two young girls in Texas. The CDC readily acknowledged those deaths at the time based on information from state health departments. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Health Department reported that its measles case count has soared to 835, with 111 cases in the last seven days. Two-thirds of those cases are in adults, and 164 people have been hospitalized in the state. Nearly all people who have been diagnosed with measles are unvaccinated. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are typically given around ages 1 and 5 and offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life. During measles outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old can receive booster doses. 9:33 Governor Shapiro speaks after first 2 Pa. residents in 35 years die of measles Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro touted the effectiveness of the MMR vaccine to combat measles after the first two unvaccinated residents of the state in 35 years were confirmed to have died of measles. supplementary_news.content_title: Measles alert issued after infected passenger travels through Stockton station
supplementary_news.content: California health officials are warning travelers about a potential measles exposure after an unvaccinated passenger infected with the virus passed through multiple counties aboard Amtrak trains and connecting buses earlier this month — including San Joaquin County and the Stockton station. The California Department of Public Health said the traveler moved through Los Angeles, Kern, San Joaquin, Butte, Sacramento and Alameda counties before continuing on to Colorado. San Joaquin County officials are urging anyone who may have shared transportation with the passenger or visited the same stations to monitor for symptoms, especially if they are unvaccinated, immunocompromised, pregnant or caring for young children. The traveler arrived in Los Angeles from Chicago on Sept. 12, then traveled through Bakersfield, Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville before departing California for Denver. Health officials identified several Amtrak train and bus routes where exposures may have occurred: Train #5717: Los Angeles to Bakersfield, Sept. 12 Train #717: Bakersfield to Stockton, Sept. 12 Train #3717: Stockton to Oroville, Sept. 12 Train #3718: Oroville to Sacramento, Sept. 13 Train #749: Sacramento to Emeryville, Sept. 13 Train #6: Emeryville to Denver, departing Sept. 14 Officials also said exposure may have occurred at stations and transit centers along those routes. Anyone who rode those trains or was present in the stations during those times should watch for symptoms for up to 21 days after possible exposure. California has reported 59 measles cases across 13 counties as of Sept. 14, according to state health officials. Nearly all cases involved people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. The latest exposure alert comes amid a nationwide measles resurgence. Public health experts have linked many recent outbreaks to declining vaccination rates and international travel. Because measles is among the most contagious diseases known, a single infected person can spread the virus to as many as nine out of 10 unvaccinated people they encounter. Health officials continue to say that the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine remains the most effective protection against the disease. Two doses provide long-lasting immunity for most people. Dr. Rita Nguyen, California's assistant state public health officer, said the exposure serves as another reminder of the importance of vaccination, particularly for young children and people with weakened immune systems. "Measles is one of the most contagious infections that can lead to severe life-long consequences including permanent brain damage and can also be fatal, especially for children," Dr. Nguyen said. Symptoms typically develop seven to 21 days after exposure and may include: An unexplained rash that spreads across the body Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or even breathes. The virus can remain suspended in the air and linger in a room for up to an hour after the infected person leaves. UC Davis pediatric infectious disease specialist Dr. Dean Blumberg noted that direct contact is not required for transmission, making measles especially difficult to contain among unvaccinated populations. Monitor for fever, rash, or other symptoms for 21 days after exposure. Contact your health care provider if you are unvaccinated or unsure of your vaccination status. Call ahead before visiting a doctor's office, urgent care clinic or hospital if you develop symptoms. Review your vaccination records and discuss MMR vaccination with your provider if needed. People who have received the recommended two doses of the MMR vaccine are generally considered protected and face a significantly lower risk of infection. For most vaccinated Californians, the risk remains low. But health officials say the exposure highlights how quickly measles can spread through public transportation hubs and other crowded settings. Travelers who may have been exposed should watch for symptoms and confirm that they and their family members are up to date on vaccinations. Louis-area bars, health officials warn St. Louis Public Radio | By Rob Edwards Published Sept. 21, 2026 at 5:34 p.m. CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Measles is a highly contagious virus. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, if one person is infected, up to 9 out of 10 people nearby will also be infected if they are not protected. Health officials are warning of possible measles exposures this month at Busch Stadium and several bars and businesses in the St. Louis area. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services said Monday that people may have been exposed to measles at several locations between Sept. 12 and Sept. 14. The most prominent was at Busch Stadium, where someone with measles was present between 6 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. Sept. 12. Health officials said the person was seated in Section 141. That same day, possible exposures were reported at the Cat’s Meow in Soulard from 3:30 p.m. to 7:50 p.m. and Paddy O’s downtown from 9:30 p.m. until closing. The other locations were in Pacific and Chesterfield: Little Ireland in Pacific from 11:30 a.m. until an unknown time Sept. 13. B&H Market in Pacific from 6:30 p.m. Sept. 13 until an unknown time. Pacific Brew Haus from 8 p.m. until closing Sept. 13. Goodcents in Chesterfield from 3 p.m. until 5:15 p.m. Sept. 14. Bud’s Market in Pacific from 5:30 p.m. to 7:45 p.m. Sept. 14. The health department is asking people who were at those locations during the listed times to monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days from the time they were first exposed. The warning comes just days after St. Louis County health officials confirmed the first measles case in a county resident in two decades. The person, who was fully vaccinated, had ridden an Amtrak train to Chicago on Aug. 27. Measles is highly contagious and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after exposure, though they can appear up to 21 days afterward. Early symptoms include fever, runny nose cough and red or watery eyes, followed by the characteristic measles rash. Have a question or comment about this story? Email St. Louis Public Radio. supplementary_news.content: South Jersey Sports Varsity Living Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH NJ thus far not impacted by neighboring Pennsylvania measles outbreak Risha Inaganti Cherry Hill Courier-Post Sept. 22, 2026, 4:47 a.m. ET Measles cases are on the rise throughout the country, with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reporting 3,471 confirmed cases in 2026 as of Sept. 17. Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that spreads through the air. Cases in 2026 have spread across 47 states and U.S. jurisdictions, including New Jersey. So far this year, New Jersey has only had one confirmed case of measles in 2026. That case came in April from a Hudson County resident. Although the Garden State has remained safe from the ongoing outbreak, its neighbor right over the Delaware River is struggling, as Pennsylvania has seen 792 cases and four measles-associated deaths this year. These deaths were the first measles-related fatals for Pennsylvania in 35 years. Pennsylvania has seen measles cases in 38 counties and exposures all across the state. A handful of exposures have occurred in Philadelphia. According to the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), exposures took place at four CHOP Philadelphia hospital areas Sept. 11. There was also a potential exposure at Philadelphia International Airport on Sept. 13. Those traveling in the airport from Sept. 13 at 7:25 p.m. to Sept. 14 at 12:05 a.m. have been potentially exposed, according to officials. Affected areas include terminals B and F, as well as common areas that connect to terminals C, D and E. Despite reaching close to the state border, the New Jersey Department of Health has confirmed that there are no active exposure locations in the state at this time. The department said that measles can be best prevented with the MMR vaccine, which stands for measles, mumps and rubella. State officials are asking all residents to stay up to date on MMR vaccines, especially before travel. Those traveling internationally with an infant should talk to a pediatrician about receiving the vaccine early. Advertisement Updated: 10:19 PM EDT Sep 22, 2026 Editorial Standards i Maegan Summers Reporter Pop-up measles vaccine clinic in Lancaster County sees Plain community turnout A pop-up vaccination clinic in Peach Bottom, Pennsylvania, hosted by the state health department, provided measles vaccines to members of the Plain community and other people in the area amid rising cases statewide. Updated: 10:19 PM EDT Sep 22, 2026 Editorial Standards i Maegan Summers Reporter PEACH BOTTOM, Pa. — A pop-up vaccination clinic at the Robert Fulton Fire Company in Peach Bottom, Pennsylvania, brought members of the local Plain community together on Tuesday to receive measles vaccinations as the state works to combat a growing outbreak. Hearst Owned WGAL Peach Bottom families seek protection from measles As of Tuesday, Pennsylvania has 792 measles cases, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Advertisement Many families from the Plain community call Peach Bottom home. When WGAL visited the clinic Tuesday afternoon, we saw multiple vans and buggies bringing people of all ages to the site. Some attendees, who spoke off camera, said they came to get vaccinated because they were scared of getting sick. They explained that many people in the Plain community have contracted measles, and they wanted to protect themselves and their children. Hearst Owned WGAL Pop-up clinics expand vaccine access The Pennsylvania Department of Health, which hosted the clinic, said it is one of many pop-up vaccine clinics being held in areas with high case numbers. For privacy reasons, filming inside the clinic was not allowed. "Measles virus is among the most infectious viruses we have. It doesn't ask what your race is, what your religion is, or where you live," said Dr. Robert Bonacci, medical advisor to the secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Health. "Our outreach isn't to target a particular community. It's really focused on where the measles virus is spreading in Pennsylvania." The department emphasized that these pop-up clinics aim to make vaccines more accessible. Dr. Bonacci said, in August, the Department of Health and its providers vaccinated more than 46,000 people with the MMR vaccine. He said that, typically, they vaccinate 25,000 people in a month. Hearst Owned WGAL "These clinics help us provide information for folks, provide a forum for them to ask questions about the vaccine and to educate them about what's going on with the outbreak and with the measles," Bonacci said. "We're making it easy for folks to get vaccinated against measles, because we know here in Pennsylvania, the way that we're going to end this outbreak is by getting as many people vaccinated and fully protected against measles as we can." The health department reiterated that people who are fully vaccinated are 97% protected against measles. Officials also said they plan to hold additional pop-up vaccine clinics at partnering locations in the future. Read Full Bio Kaia Hubbard Updated on: September 20, 2026 / 3:37 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Washington — GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana on Sunday urged the president to be "radically honest" when he's speaking about vaccines, as the U.S. this year has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades. "I would just ask the president to be aware that people are listening to him — if he discourages immunization, there'll be fewer people immunized, and if we're speaking of measles, there'll be more people sick in the hospital or even die," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." The Trump administration has been encouraging parents to vaccinate their children against measles in recent months, as cases have climbed. But Mr. Trump has cast doubt on the vaccine and its schedule, including through an executive order last month suggesting that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, should be given as three separate shots. He also claimed without evidence that the MMR vaccine, if not separated, could be "lethal." Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, the president said he is going to "demand" that drug companies split up kids' vaccines into five doses, given in six-month intervals. He said, "the vaccine size will be much, much less" and argued that it will lead "to a massive reduction in autism." "So instead of having a massive dose of 82 or 88 different vaccines pumped into your arm, we'll take out certain vaccines that people are a little worried about," Mr. Trump said. Cassidy, a medical doctor, said he didn't know which vaccines the president was referencing. But he stressed that there needs to be "radical honesty." "Have the president come forward — what is he basing this on? Who's giving him advice?" Cassidy said. Cassidy said he approaches the issue "as a physician," saying people are worried, and "we need to address that worry where it is." "If you want to be radically honest, the vaccines are safe, they've been proven to be safe, and the current regimen has been timed to be most convenient to the parent," he said. "At any point, the parent can say, 'I want something different.'" Cassidy urged the president to explain his position, asking, "Why do you think this vaccine is lethal?" "Have you ever seen a case of lethality?" he said. "And what about the people who are not vaccinated, who are getting sick and even dying?" The Louisiana Republican cited recent measles-related deaths, including a 40-year-old and an 18-year-old. He said, "having measles is not a kind of victimless kind of experience," comparing it to drunk driving. "You can drink and get drunk, but if you drive, you're going to hurt other people," Cassidy said. "You can get measles, but when you start spreading it to other people, a 40-year-old dies, an 18-year-old dies, children in a neonatal intensive care unit are at risk. People have got to realize, and the government has to realize it. The president should be saying, 'Be vaccinated. It is safe and effective.'" He added, "We should have a common voice of radical honesty, of trying to help the American people understand what is safe. And if the president calls it lethal, then where are you getting your information, Mr. President? And if you really don't have it, why are you willing to risk the lives of fellow Americans?" The Louisiana Republican, who's leaving office early next year after the president endorsed his GOP challenger, chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Asked what he needs to hear from the nominee for FDA commissioner, Heidi Overton, at her hearing this week, Cassidy said, "I need to hear that she understands that calling the measles vaccine lethal is absurd, and we need radical honesty." Cassidy also noted that the president's nominee for surgeon general, Nicole Saphier, said in a committee hearing last week that the MMR vaccine is not lethal, while encouraging people to get vaccinated. Cassidy said she earned his vote. "When somebody is willing to be honest to the American people and say that vaccines are safe, you should be taking it, and the consequence of not can even include death, well, what else can you ask for when it comes to vaccines?" he said. potential exposure at Edwardsville restaurant St. Louis Public Radio | By Rob Edwards Published Sept. 23, 2026 at 2:42 p.m. CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Salt + Smoke / Facebook Salt + Smoke opened in Edwardsville in May 2026. Health officials have confirmed a case of measles in Edwardsville. The Madison County Health Department said people who were at Salt + Smoke at 410 N. Main St. in Edwardsville between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. Sept. 10 may have been exposed to measles. Anyone who was at that location during that time should monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days after the potential exposure, according to the health department. Symptoms of measles can include fever, cough, runny nose and the characteristic red rash that starts around the head or face and spreads to the rest of the body. People who were potentially exposed and develop symptoms should contact their medical provider. Health officials say they should call in advance before arriving so medical facilities can take precautions to prevent additional exposures. Missouri health officials notified the public on Monday about another case of measles in the St. Louis region. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services said people may have been exposed to measles at several locations between Sept. 12 and Sept. 14. The most prominent place was Busch Stadium, where someone with measles was present between 6 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. Sept. 12. Health officials said the infected person also visited several bars and businesses in St. Louis, Chesterfield and Pacific. Have a question or comment about this story? Email St. Louis Public Radio. California officials warn of possible measles exposure in 6 counties due to infected Amtrak rider KCRA / KQCA US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:57 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 8:45 PM PDT Sep 21, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jeremiah Martinez Digital Producer Denzen Cortez Reporter California officials warn of possible measles exposure in 6 counties due to infected Amtrak rider Updated: 8:45 PM PDT Sep 21, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jeremiah Martinez Digital Producer Denzen Cortez Reporter State public health officials are warning about a possible measles exposure across multiple California counties after an infected passenger traveled across the country on trains and buses. The California Department of Public Health said the unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state using Amtrak trains and thruway buses with transfers in at least six counties: Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin. Advertisement Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. People who are not vaccinated, particularly young children and pregnant people, face the highest risk of severe illness and even death, according to officials. The passenger arrived in California from an Amtrak train to Los Angeles on Sept. 10, according to officials. After arriving in Los Angeles, they took a route to Bakersfield and then went to Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento, and Emeryville before leaving the state to Denver. Here is the route the passenger took: Sept. 10: Departed Chicago at 1:30 p.m. Sept. 12: Arrived at Los Angeles Union Station on Sept. 12 at 8:12 a.m. Sept. 12: Departed Los Angles at 10:55 a.m. and arrived at Bakersfield station at 1;45 p.m. Sept. 12: Departed Bakersfield at 2:02 p.m. and arrived at Stockton—San Joaquin St Station at 6:29 p.m. Sept. 12: Departed Stockton at 6:35 p.m. and arrived at Oroville bus/thruway stop at 9:30 p.m. Sept. 13: Departed Oroville at 4 p.m. and arrived to Sacramento Valley Station at 6:05 p.m. Sept. 13: Departed Sacramento at 6:53 p.m. and arrived to Emeryville Station at 8:36 p.m. Sept. 14: Departed Emeryville at 8:25 a.m. and arrived to Denver at 6:59 p.m. Officials said people who were passengers on those trains or buses or who were at the stations on those days have been exposed to measles. Officials added it's working with federal partners and local health departments to notify people who may have been exposed. "This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles," Assistant State Public Health Officer Dr. Rita Nguyen said in a statement. "The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated." KCRA 3’s Denzen Cortez spoke with Dr. Dean Blumberg, professor and chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UC Davis Health, who said measles can spread without direct contact with an infected person. “The issue with measles is it's likely the most contagious infection known to humans,” Blumberg said. “You don't even have to be in the same room at the same time with somebody to get measles, since the virus can linger in the air for an hour or two after they left.” Blumberg said vaccination dramatically changes the risk for someone who may have been exposed. “If they've been vaccinated, the good news is that they're protected and they're immune,” Blumberg said. “If they're not vaccinated, then measles has about a 90% attack rate, meaning there's a nine times out of ten chance that somebody is going to get infected.” As of Sept. 14, 2026, a total of 59 measles cases have been reported in 13 counties in California, according to officials. Patients were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status in 94 percent of cases. What to do if you have been exposed or have symptoms Officials said to monitor symptoms, such as watching for a fever and/or unexplained rash from seven to 21 days after exposure. If symptoms develop, officials urged people to call your doctor for guidance. If anyone suspects they have measles, it's recommended to call their health care provider before visiting any health care facility to avoid exposing others. People who are not vaccinated against measles or are unsure of their status are recommended to contact their doctor about receiving the vaccine. Two doses of the vaccine are needed to be fully immunized, officials said. Measles virus. 3D illustration showing structure of measles virus with surface glycoprotein spikes heamagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion protein Dr_Microbe - stock.adobe.com Clark County Public Health is investigating two cases of measles in unvaccinated children. The cases were reported on September 23. People who were at a Battle Ground school may have been exposed. According to the health department, a person who tested positive visited River HomeLink on Southwest Eaton Boulevard on September 17. They were there from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Clark County Public Health is working with Battle Ground Public Schools to identify students and staff who are not protected against measles. Those individuals will be excluded from school, child care and other settings for 21 days. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Anyone who was at the school and has not been vaccinated against measles or has not had measles in the past is at risk for getting sick. The health department recommends staying home and out of public places for three weeks. During that time, anyone who believes they have symptoms of measles should call their health care provider before visiting the medical office to make a plan that avoids exposing others.
