Griffen Smith Lee Enterprises 2 min read An electron microscope image of a measles virus particle on Feb. 4, 2015. Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Loading Audio Player By Instaread, Please Wait... http://www.bozemandailychronicle.com offers audio versions of articles using Instaread. Some words may be mispronounced. A person infected with measles who visited Flathead County potentially exposed the public at three separate locations from Sept. 8 to Sept. 11, health department officials announced Sunday. Flathead County is asking those exposed at the public locations to monitor their symptoms for 21 days, as measles is a highly contagious viral disease that causes a high fever and a red blotchy skin rash. “We are awaiting test results for a suspected case and anticipate that additional exposure sites may be identified,” health officials said in the announcement. The following locations were confirmed as potential exposure areas for the disease. The exposure period can last up to two hours as measles can stay airborne after an infected person leaves the area. Glacier Highland — Gift Store and Restaurant 12555 Highway 2 E., West Glacier, MT, 59936 Sept. 8-Sept. 11 Logan Health Primary Care 1675 Talbot Road, Columbia Falls, MT, 59912 Sept. 8 from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m. Amtrack Train No. 8 traveling eastbound from West Glacier Sept. 11 The Flathead City-County Health Department asked those who are potentially exposed to complete a measles exposure self-assessment on the department’s website. If someone has symptoms of measles, officials recommend calling a healthcare provider immediately and asked people to stay home until one is no longer contagious or measles are rules out as the illness. The prevalence of measles has increased by more than 1,000 cases nationwide compared to 2025, according to data from John Hopkins University. In Montana, five people in Helena tested positive for measles in March, and one person infected with measles visited Missoula County in November 2025, the Missoulian reported. People immune through vaccination, lab-confirmed immunity or prior infection, or those born before 1957 are generally not considered at risk for infection, the health department said. Meanwhile, those who are unvaccinated from measles have a 90% chance of infection if exposed to the disease. “Measles is a very contagious disease that spreads mainly through the air,” the health department said. “When an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, tiny droplets containing the virus are released and can remain in the air for up to two hours. This means someone can get measles even without direct contact with the infected person.” Measles usually starts with a fever, cough or runny nose and red eyes. Small white spots can also appear inside the cheeks. About seven to 14 days after exposure, a red rash appears, beginning on the face and then spreading to the rest of the body. The best way to prevent measles is through vaccination, according to the health department. A standards measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is about 97% effective. People interested in vaccination can contact their healthcare provider or schedule an appointment with the heath department online or by calling 406-751-8110. Griffen Smith is the local government reporter for the Missoulian. He is a 2023 graduate of the University of Montana School of Journalism and previously served as the editor of the Seeley Swan Pathfinder. Posted 6:50 PM, Sep 22, 2026 and last updated 7:10 PM, Sep 22, 2026 The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) on Tuesday announced one new confirmed case of measles in the state. The case is in Chippewa County, and at this time, DHS said there are no reports of public exposures associated with it. Since August, DHS said confirmed measles cases have also been reported in Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, Marathon and Vernon counties. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Measles is a highly contagious disease that can be spread from person to person through the air and can stay in the air for two hours after a sick person coughs or sneezes. It can cause serious health complications, including pneumonia, brain damage and deafness, and can sometimes be deadly, according to DHS. If you develop symptoms, DHS advises residents to call a health care provider, even if they are not aware of a specific exposure. Symptoms of measles typically appear 10 to 21 days after exposure to the virus. Let's talk: Hey there! supplementary_news.content_title: Potential measles exposure in St. Louis area after third case linked to train ride
supplementary_news.content: ST. LOUIS, Mo. — There are now at least three measles cases linked to an exposure on a train in Missouri. The original case was in Jackson County, the second case in St. Louis County and a third person in Franklin County has become infected. The third patient visited several locations around St. Louis between Sept. 12-14. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services (DHSS), along with local health officials, are warning about possible measles exposure at those locations. Below are listed the date, times and locations of where exposure may have been possible: - Sept. 12 between 3:30 p.m. and 7:50 p.m. at The Cat's Meow in Soulard - Sept. 12 between 6 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. at Busch Stadium in section 141 - Sept. 12 between 9:30 p.m. and closing of Paddy O's - Sept. 13 from 11:30 to an unknown time in Little Ireland in Pacific, Mo. - Sept. 13 from 6:30 p.m. to an unknown time at B&H market in Pacific, Mo. - Sept. 13 from 8 p.m. until close at Pacific Brew House in Pacific, Mo. - Sept. 14 from 3 p.m. to 5:15 p.m. a Goodcents in Chesterfield, Mo. - Sept. 14 from 5:30 p.m. until 7:45 p.m. at Bud's Market in Pacific, Mo. The patients are linked to an exposure that happened on a train that left Sedalia on its way to Chicago in August. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that typically begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. One person with measles can easily pass it on to 9 out of 10 people around them who are unvaccinated or do not have natural immunity, the DHSS said in a press release. Symptoms typically appear 7-14 days after contact with the virus. Tiny white spots may appear inside the mouth 2-3 days after symptoms begin. Measles rash appears 3 to 5 days after the first symptoms. It usually begins as flat, red spots that appear on the face at the hairline. They then spread downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs and feet. Exposed individuals should monitor for measles symptoms for 21 days from the date of exposure and contact their local public health agency if symptoms appear. People who think they have measles should isolate themselves and call their health care provider before arriving to be tested. More information about measles and county-level MMR vaccination rates can be found at Health.Mo.Gov/Measles
